ORDER 


1. This is a complaint filed by the complainant u/s 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 raising the 
following contentions: - 


The complainant was appointed by the opposite party in the post of MCS / Office Assistant 
(Multipurpose) / Substaff at their B G Kere branch on 01.06.2009. He submitted application and documents and 
attended interview for selection. Since then he worked continuously in the said branch till the date of his 
termination / retrenchment / discharge / dismissal of his service on 20.06.2014. As a part of his job, he used to 
open the branch by collecting keys from the Manager, cleaning the office, aiding the customers and the branch in 
various ways. In order to avoid the extension of status and benefits of permanent workman to him, the Opposite 
Party directed the B G Kere branch to debit his wages as coolie charges to the General ledger account without 
obtaining his signature on the debit vouchers. The officials of the branch took his signature on the overleaf of 
coolie paid debit vouchers along with the signatures of the branch officers while paying wages in cash to him. He 
was the only person doing the work of the office attendant / messenger / sweeper / substaff / daily wager / MCS 
etc on coolie charges. The Opposite Party was not marking attendance register for his work, not extended 
payment register to him, signing debit vouchers for his wages by the officers of the bank and receiving amount 
by them and then paying the amounts to him as wages, debiting the wages paid to him to General Charges 
Account instead of salary paid account / Establishment charges, not issuing appointment orders or certificates for 
the services rendered by him in the bank, refusal to pay wages applicable to messengers / housekeeping staff / 
sub staff / MCS to him, not extending the service benefits applicable to permanent workman, taking work from 
him for years together as Coolie by terming his wages as coolie charges practiced by the opposite party are all 
unfair labour practices under the 5" Schedule of the ID Act 1947. The complainant along with other coolie 
workers of the opposite party bank formed a union called Pragathi Grameena Bank Daily Wage Workers Union 
in 2012 and he was active in the Union activities. The Union filed cases before the Central Labour Machinery for 
getting the benefits for the daily wage workers of the Bank. This has caused annoyance to the then management 
against him. CR 22/2013 is pending before this Tribunal in which the Union raised a dispute for regularization of 
services of the workmen including him. He is directly connected with the said dispute raised by the said union. 
On 20.06.2014, the Branch Manager Mr. Chinappa became hostile to him for having brought tea already kept 
made from the nearby tea shop instead of fresh tea. The Branch Manager asked him not to come for work 
anymore in a fit of anger. Despite his repeated request, the Manager did not change his stand. Thus he was 
terminated abruptly for the above flimsy reason and without issuing any notice to him or paying any 
retrenchment compensation. The opposite party has not filed any application before the appropriate Government 
seeking permission to retrench him u/s 25 N of the ID Act 1947. Therefore, the retrenchment of his service is 
illegal, ab-initio void and he is deemed to be in the services of the Bank as per sec 25 N(7) of the ID Act. As per 
the provision of Sec 33 of the ID Act, the opposite party cannot alter or change the conditions of his service 
applicable to him immediately before the commencement of the proceedings of C R 22/2013 to his prejudice , 
during the pendency of CR 22/2013 before this Tribunal without the expressed permission in writing from the 
tribunal and also shall not discharge / dismiss / terminate / retrench him unless he was paid wages for one month 
and without making an application for approval of the action so taken. The opposite party has not observed any 
of the provisions of the ID Act 1947 and has not filed any application before the Tribunal. The action of the 
opposite party is against the provisions of the ID Act, principles of natural justice, illegal, null and void. The 
opposite party was paying him wages @ Rs. 3600/- per month. The opposite party has not paid any wages to him 
since the retrenchment of his services. Since the opposite party has not filed any application before the Tribunal 
seeking approval of their action, he is entitled for payment of full wages drawn by him every month till the 
disposal of this case. Since the opposite party has not filed any application before the appropriate government for 
the termination of his services, not issued any copy of such application to him nor any notice / notice pay / 
compensation as required u/s 25 N of the ID Act, he is deemed to be in service for the benefits as applicable to 
him prior to such cessation of his service and is entitled for wages as per sec 25N (7) of the ID Act. Due to the 
illegal cessation of service imposed on him by the opposite party, the complainant and his family are suffering 
economically and socially. Hence this complaint for declaring the termination / retrenchment / discharge / 
dismissal of the complainant from 20.06.2014 is not in accordance with the provisions of the ID Act 1947, 
against the principles of natural justice, arbitrary, unilateral, ill motivated and illegal and to direct the opposite 
party to reinstate the complainant with full back wages, continuity of service with regularization, ancillary 
benefits from 20.06.2014 and with cost. 


2. The opposite party at the outset has contended that the complainant has no enforceable cause of action to 
raise Industrial Dispute and has no right to seek employment in the bank and there is no discharge or termination 
of employment and hence no Industrial Dispute lie under Industrial Disputes Act 1947. It is equally contended 
that there is no post of messenger cum sweeper in the bank. The opposite party inter alia contended that based on 
the man power requirement assessed by the bank as per the guidelines issued by the Government of India at the 
end of March every year, the total vacancies to be filled up by the direct recruitment and promotions will be 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 63 


identified and the process of direct recruitment and promotions will be initiated after obtaining permissions from 
the Sponsor Bank viz., Canara Bank and the Board of the opposite party bank. Recruitment and appointment of 
employees in the Regional Rural Banks is governed by the rules framed by the Government of India vide 
notification dated 13.07.2010 called “Regional Rural Banks (Appointment and Promotions of Officers and 
Employees) Rules 2010”. As per the said rules, procedure with regard to Office Attendant (Multipurpose Group 
C employees) are prescribed, the selection process being on the basis of interview to be conducted by a 
Committee. The branches / offices of the bank engage coolies occasionally and intermittently as and when 
necessitated for doing menial works in the branches. In order to meet the exigencies of the work, the opposite 
party bank branches used to engage coolies only for few hours for such menial works like cleaning, sweeping 
and watering and were paid coolie charges proportionately depending upon the number of hours they worked. 
The complainant was also engaged similarly as a coolie intermittently and not continuously. Depending upon the 
availability of the person in the locale, the Branch Manager engaged such person on need basis for such works. 
As per the Government of India guidelines for appointment of Regular Attendants, the names should be 
sponsored by the employment exchange / Sainik Board and such engagement is also subject to the conditions 
stipulated in regard to educational qualification, age etc. While engaging the coolies, no educational 
qualifications or age were looked into and whoever is available locally would be engaged to carry out such 
emergent / menial casual work. The complainant might have been engaged by the Branch Manager for such 
casual works but not continuously. Such casual engagements will not give any enforceable course of action for 
the relief sought for and no locus standi to file this Complaint. They are not governed by any rules and regulation 
of the bank and there is no employee employer relationship as they have not been engaged by the bank against 
the post. It is the settled position in law that a person engaged intermittently on daily wages will not have the 
right to be absorbed for any post. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in State of Karnataka vs. Uma Devi 
have laid down the law relating to regularization / permanency claims of casual employees. The opposite party 
bank is constituted under the RRB Act, the recruitment and appointment in the Bank is governed by the rules 
framed u/s 29 of the said Act. The complainant has not undergone any process for recruitment / appointment as 
per the said rules. The contention of the complainant that he was appointed by the opposite party at their B G 
Kere branch on 01.06.2009 by taking application form etc. is denied. The Branch Manager has no power to 
recruit / appoint any employee. The complainant was engaged only occasionally to attend to menial / urgent 
works and not continuously. Since the complainant was not recruited / appointed by the opposite party anytime, 
his termination / dismissal / retrenchment on 20.06.2014 did not arise. Consequently, question of issuing notice 
to him, payment of retrenchment compensation, payment of wages of one month, filing of application before the 
Tribunal before or during the pendency of CR 22/2013 and seeking permission u/s 25N of the Act does not arise. 
Under the circumstances, sec 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act has no application in his case. He was never 
engaged on a continuous basis nor for attending the regular functions of substaff. He was paid wages for the 
occasional / casual works he was engaged to. He was not governed by any service conditions in the opposite 
party banks and hence no question of altering or changing the conditions of service arises. Sec 33 of the ID Act, 
in the circumstances has no relevance in his case. The complainant has not been appointed in the payrolls of the 
opposite party at any time. Since he has not been appointed in the opposite party bank, question of marking in 
the attendance register, extending payment registered to him, debiting the payment made to him to salary 
account, issuing appointment orders, issuing certificates and denying benefits etc. did not arise. Hence the 
allegation of unfair labour practice on the part of the II Party is untenable. The contention of the complainant that 
his involvement in the union activities and filing of Industrial Dispute by the said union for getting benefits to 
the daily wage workers has caused anger to the opposite party is a figment of his imagination and hence denied. 
The complainant was not working in the opposite party bank on continuous basis and was engaged occasionally , 
casually for menial and urgent requirements. His contention that he was being paid wages @ Rs. 3600/- is 
denied. The incident narrated in para 9 of the complaint regarding alleged fetching of rotten tea is far from truth 
and is only self-serving statement. His contentions that he was deemed to be in service and entitled for benefits 
are untenable and baseless. The complainant has not undergone any process of recruitment and is not entitled for 
recruitment for appointment in the opposite party bank or for reinstatement or other ancillary benefits as claimed 
by him. For all these reasons, the opposite party has prayed for rejection of the complaint. 


3. From the above rival pleadings, following points arise for consideration: - 
1. Whether the complaint is legally and factually maintainable? 


2. Whether the Complainant is proved to have been working continuously in the opposite party 
establishment since 01.06.2009? 


3. Whether the complainant is proved to have been discharged / terminated / retrenched / dismissed 
from service as contended by him? 


4. Whether the alleged contravention of the provision of sec 33 of the ID Act is proved by the 
complainant? 


5. Whether the complainant is entitled to get reinstatement to the service with full back wages, 


64 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


continuity of service and ancillary benefits from 20.06.2014 as prayed for? 
6. What is the proper Order and Award to be passed in this complaint case? 
4. — Either of the parties did not prefer to adduce any evidence in the matter. 
5. Heard the oral and written arguments submitted from both sides. 


6. Points no. 1 to 4:- Since all these points are closely integrated and inter-twined, all these points are 
discussed together. Alleging contravention of the provisions of sec 33 of the ID Act 1947, the complainant filed 
the instant complaint u/s 33A of the Act on the factual averment that the opposite party has not filed any 
application before this Tribunal seeking permission for retrenching / terminating / dismissing him on 20.06.2014 
and not filing any application for approval of their said action. The complainant’s case is that he was appointed 
by the opposite party bank at their B G Kere branch on 01.06.2009 on submission of application and subjecting 
him for interview and on obtaining documents from him. He claims that since then he has worked continuously 
in the said branch on all working days. It is his further case that to his surprise, for just a flimsy reason that he 
could not adhere to the mandate of the then Manager of the B G Kere branch to fetch fresh tea from the nearby 
tea shop as the shop vendor gave him only a cup of tea already available there, he was kicked out from his job. 
Without giving any prior notice and bereft of any valid reason, he was asked on 20.06.2014 not to come for work 
and his services are terminated. The complainant inter alia pleaded that he is an active member in a Union under 
the name and style Pragathi Grameena Bank Daily Wage Workers Union formed between himself with other 
coolie workers of the opposite party bank. The said union has raised a dispute for regularization of the service of 
the complainant and other similarly placed coolie before the Central Government Machinery and the same is 
registered and pending before this Tribunal as CR 22/2013. It is the case of the complainant that he is directly 
connected with the said dispute raised by the Union pending before this Tribunal. The disengagement of job on 
20.06.2014 according to the complainant tantamounts to contravention of the provisions of sec 33 of the ID Act 
as according to him it happened when the industrial dispute raised by the union for and on behalf of him and the 
other coolie workers was pending adjudication. This gave way for filing this complaint u/s 33A of the ID Act. 


7. Oral and written arguments are advanced on behalf of the complainant narrating all these events by his 
authorized representative. 


8. The learned counsel for the opposite party per contra put forth his rival submission that the complainant has 
never ever rendered any continuous service in the opposite party bank. Instead the bank was in the practice of 
engaging persons from the locale for attending menial job like sweeping, cleaning and watering when the regular 
employees are absent or proceed on leave and such persons were paid coolie charges for the same. According to 
the opposite party, the complainant was also so casually engaged depending on the requirement of the branch as 
a coolie for doing menial works and such works carried out by him was not regular in nature, but only on need 
basis. To put it differently, according to the opposite party the engagement of the complainant was not 
continuous and it was only intermittent. 


9. Ofcourse, the event of non-engagement for work said to have happened on 20.06.2014 is apparently during 
the pendency of CR 22/2013. However the complainant did not prefer to bring home any proof that he was in 
service in the opposite party bank even on the previous day or anytime there-before in a constant and continuous 
stretch so as to establish the retrenchment / dismissal / discharge / termination alleged in the complaint. Here it is 
contextually profitable to quote Sec 33 of the Act: 


33. [ Conditions of service, etc., to remain unchanged under certain circumstances during pendency of 
proceedings. ] 


(1)During the pendency of any conciliation proceeding before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any 
proceeding before ][an arbitrator or] [a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal in respect of an 
industrial dispute, no employer shall- (a)in regard to any matter connected with the dispute, alter, to the 
prejudice of the workmen concerned in such dispute, the conditions of service applicable to them immediately 
before the commencement of such proceeding; or (b)for any misconduct connected with the dispute, discharge 
or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, any workmen concerned in such dispute, ave with the express 
permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending.(2)During the pendency of any 
such proceeding in respect of an industrial dispute, the employer may, in accordance with the standing orders 
applicable to a workman concerned in such dispute ] [or, where there are no such standing orders, in 
accordance with the terms of the contract, whether express or implied, between him and the workman] (a)[{ 
alter, in regard to any matter not connected with the dispute, the conditions of service applicable to that 
workman immediately before the commencement of such proceeding; or (b) for any misconduct not connected 
with the dispute, discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, that workman: Provided that no such 
workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one month and an application 
has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending for approval of the 
action taken by the employer. (3)Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (2), no employer shall, 
during the pendency of any such proceeding in respect of an industrial dispute, take any action against any 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 65 


protected workman concerned in such dispute (a) by altering, to the prejudice of such protected workman, the 
conditions of service applicable to him immediately before the commencement of such proceedings; or (b) by 
discharging or punishing, whether by dismissal or otherwise, such protected workman, save with the express 
permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending. Explanation:-For the purposes 
of this sub-section, a "protected workman ", in relation to an establishment, means a workman who, being] [a 
member of the executive or other office bearer] [of a registered trade union connected with the establishment, 
is recognised as such in accordance with rules made in this behalf.(4)In every establishment, the number of 
workmen to be recognised as protected workmen for the purposes of sub-section (3) shall be one per cent. of 
the total number of workmen employed therein subject to a minimum number of five protected workmen and a 
maximum number of one hundred protected workmen and for the aforesaid purpose, the appropriate 
Government may make rules providing for the distribution of such protected workmen among various trade 
unions, if any, connected with the establishment and the manner in which the workmen may be chosen and 
recognised as protected workmen.(5)Where an employer makes an application to a conciliation officer, Board, 
] [an arbitrator, a] [Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal under the proviso to sub-section (2) for 
approval of the action taken by him, the authority concerned shall, without delay, hear such application and 
pass, ] [within a period of three months from the date of receipt of such application] [ Substituted by Act 46 of 
1982, Section 17, for " as expeditiously as possible" (w.e.f. 21.8.1984).][, such order in relation thereto as it 
deems fit:]. ][Provided that where any such authority considers it necessary or expedient so to do, it may, for 
reasons to be recorded in writing, extend such period by such further period as it may think fit: Provided 
further that no proceedings before any such authority shall lapse merely on the ground that any period 
specified in this sub-section had expired without such proceedings being completed. ] 


10. Of course by enacting sec 33, the legislature wanted to ensure a fair and satisfactory enquiry of the 
industrial dispute undisturbed by any action on the part of the employer or the employee likely to create fresh 
cause for disharmony between them. The legislature visualized that during the pendency of the industrial dispute 
status quo should be maintained and no further element of discord should be introduced between the employer 
and the employee. The objective of the provision of sec 33 is to put a ban on the prerogative of the employer in 
altering the service condition of the employee pending enquiry of the industrial dispute raised by them. The 
primary principle is that if an Industrial Dispute is raised by a group of workmen acting on their own through 
their union, the general conclusion is that the all those who sponsored the dispute are concerned in it. However 
the very factum of raising an Industrial Dispute and pendency of such a dispute in a court of law by an individual 
employee or a group of employees by itself does not lead to the inference that such an individual who alleges 
retrenchment from services was a workman in continuous service under the employer, unless proved by concrete 
evidence. Indeed, Sec 33A stands to the rescue of a workman who alleges alteration or cessation of service by 
the employer during the pendency of an Industrial Dispute. A regular workman / employee or a casual employee 
on a continuing basis under an employer who files a complaint u/s 33A certainly stands on a different footing 
than the one who claims continuity of service as a casual labourer and whose claim is not accepted by the 
employer. 


11. The case on hand portrays the scenario the employer disowns and denies the complainant as its regular 
daily wager. The alleged retrenchment of service dated 20.06.2014 averred by the complainant is not accepted or 
recognized by the Oppose Party in the given case. The definite stand of the opposite party is that the complainant 
had been engaged very occasionally and intermittently on need basis to attend menial works like sweeping, 
cleaning etc. without touching the routine works in the office. The complainant per contra very particularly 
pleaded that apart from cleaning in and around the bank office, he was entrusted with the task of assisting 
customers in making challans for cash / cheque, deposits taking and keeping cash in double lock, writing 
registers, collecting cash from other banks from the cheques drawn on them, printing passbooks, deposit receipts, 
writing loan papers, making deposit mobilization, bundling payment slips and day book and such so many tasks. 
However according to the opposite party all the above works are the routine tasks of the regular employees and 
not of such casual workers engaged for attending menial jobs. Thus the factual pleadings of the complainant 
indicate that his engagement in the opposite party bank was not to attend menial labour alone but higher tasks as 
well, as mentioned above. It is while attending such highly responsible tasks in his so called status as MCS / 
Office assistant (multipurpose) / sub-staff at the B G Kere branch of the opposite party continuously since 
01.06.2009 that the opposite party has terminated / retrenched his services on 20.06.2014. This factum also the 
opposite party has emphatically opposed and disputed. According to the opposite party, no such retrenchment or 
termination has ever occurred nor was there any occasion for that as the bank had not engaged the complainant 
in such a position at all in work continuously. In this factual background it is the primary duty of the complainant 
to substantiate that his very entry in the bank was on 01.06.2009 and he continued to perform services in the 
opposite party bank without any break till 20.06.2014. The complainant is equally obliged to prove that he was 
disengaged from a continuous service on 20.06.2014. Inability to offer menial job on a particular date when there 
was no requirement to engage a casual labourer to attend such work pleaded by the opposite party does oblige 
the complainant to substantiate his specific case by adducing reliable and concrete material evidence establishing 
all the aspects pleaded by him in the complaint. The mere pleading raised by him regarding the prevalence / 


66 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


pendency of an Industrial Dispute and the so called termination or retrenchment of services on 20.06.2014 
without bringing home any iota of evidence substantiating the above plea does not bind this Tribunal to accept 
the case set forth by him as gospel truth and to draw a finding against the opposite party. 


12. It is the settled position of law that u/s 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, the complainant carries the 
initial burden / onus to prove that the employer contravened sec 33 of the Act and such contravention occurred 
during the pendency of a dispute, by presenting the facts supported by evidence. Once the complainant 
discharges his initial burden to establish that he is an employee in continuous service within the parameters of 
sec 33 of the Act and such contravention occurred as pleaded and proved, the employer must then justify their 
actions especially concerning alleged dismissal / retrenchment / termination, often leading to the tribunal 
deciding if the action was fair and just like any other Industrial Dispute. 


13. Here in the given case, the one and only aspect accepted and admitted by the opposite party is the pendency 
of CR 22/2013 raised by the Daily Workers Union. That by itself does not discharge the onus of proof cast on the 
complainant to prima facie establish its case. The alleged contravention of service conditions or an illegal 
cessation of the service of an employee by the employer is not an aspect to be simply inferred by the Tribunal 
out of nothing but to be very precisely, meticulously and scrupulously proved and established by the aggrieved 
complainant. 


14. Sec 33A is designed to provide an instant remedy to a workman aggrieved by the contravention of sec 33 
by filing a complaint before adjudicatory authorities or conciliatory authorities. It is trite that where such a 
complaint is made to an adjudicatory authority viz. Labour Court / Tribunal, it will adjudicate upon the dispute 
as if it is a dispute referred to or pending before it, so that the workman is saved of the botheration of moving the 
Government for referring this dispute for adjudication. 


15. The basic question to be considered by this Tribunal in the complaint on hand u/s 33A is whether there has 
been a contravention by the employer of the provisions of sec 33 and in the event it is found that there has been a 
contravention of the provisions, then to embark upon the exercise to adjudicate about the matter so complained 
of in the complaint on its merit. No written order of termination / retrenchment is produced by the complainant to 
justify his pleadings. Of course, he averred in the complaint that the termination issued by the opposite party was 
only oral. If that be so, it should be proved by the complainant that he was in continuous service under the 
opposite party and was subjected for a termination / retrenchment on an oral order by mounting the witness box. 
Going by the proceedings underwent in the given case, it is clear that once the statement of objection is filed by 
the opposite party, the matter was posted for evidence of the complainant and on the repeated request of the 
complainant, evidence / enquiry was postponed by my learned predecessor by not less than 5 occasions. Then at 
the whimsical stand of the complainant it is made out that there is no need to adduce evidence and the matter be 
posted for arguments. In fact, as per law, before giving any relief to the aggrieved employee under the section, 
the authority viz., this Tribunal has first to determine that the employee was continuously working under the 
employer and the latter had surreptitiously kicked out him from the job without complying with the mandate u/s 
33 of the Act. Hence a contravention of sec 33 is the foundation for exercise of the power u/s 33A of the Act. As 
already observed and as rightly pointed out by the learned counsel for the opposite party, no reliable proof / 
evidence is brought on record by the complainant to substantiate that there is contravention of provisions of sec 
33 of the Act from the side of the opposite party. 


16. In the event if the alleged factum of infraction from the provision of sec 33 is established, the matter has to 
be very meticulously adjudicated on merit to examine whether the complainant is entitled to get an order of 
reinstatement. It is trite that even when contravention of sec 33 is established, that does not automatically lead to 
an order for reinstatement. So, at large, the complainant is at the task to prove and establish the primary elements 
viz., his status as a daily wage employee under the opposite party coupled with contravention of the provisions of 
sec 33 by the latter and then his eventual right to get reinstatement to service with equivalent benefits. 
Determination of all these issues by the legal forum could be possible only when reliable evidence is adduced by 
the complainant by offering himself for searching cross examination by the opposite party in a full-fledged trial. 
It is trite that the initial burden lies on the employee to prove that he falls under the definition of a “workman” 
under the Industrial Disputes Act. If the employee presents a strong prima facie case, the management must then 
provide evidence to rebut it. Of course, the evidence to be adduced by the person claiming to be an employee 
must be substantial, often a preponderance of evidence depending on the claim. It is no longer res-integra that the 
burden of proving the employer-employee relationship primarily rest upon the person who asserts its existence. 
In a situation where a person asserts to be an employee of the management which the management denies, the 
duty primarily rests upon the person so asserting to give positive evidence in his favour and discharge his initial 
burden. At the risk of repetition I say, once such a person has given such a positive evidence in his favour, only 
then the burden would shift on the management to give evidence to counter such claims, because it is always 
possible to prove positive facts than a negative. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Workman of Nilgiri Co-Op 
Mkt Society LTD vs. State of Tamil Nadu (AIR 2004 SC 1639) held that it is a well settled principle of law 
that the person who is setting up a plea of existence of relationship of employer and employee, the burden would 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 67 


be upon him. Similar view is adopted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bank of Baroda vs. Ghemarabhai 
Harijibhai Rabari (2005 (10) SCC 792). The complainant herein kept aloof from trial feeling shy of an 
intensive quiz in the witness box. Probably, the complainant might have been misled, misguided or mal-advised 
not to mount the witness box so as to avoid probable inconvenience of a grilling cross-examination. The net 
result of such willful avoidance of requisite procedure by the complainant either by himself or as instilled upon 
him is complete failure of the case projected by him. 


17. Extensive argument is advanced on behalf of the complainant with the aid of plethora of legal authorities 
canvassing for a favorable order of reinstatement with full back wages, continuity of service with regularization 
and ancillary benefits from 20.06.2014. As could be heard from Learned Counsel for the opposite party, all these 
wider reliefs sought for by the complainant are the main reliefs claimed in the said case CR 22/2013. By 
consciously avoiding to give oral or documentary evidence in this case, what is craved for on behalf of the 
complainant is to grant the above reliefs even without facing a trial. Granting such reliefs in his favour without 
providing / supplementing any sort of evidentiary support would tantamount to prejudging the issue raised in the 
Industrial Dispute case CR 22/2013 in a very shortcut method. 


18. Argument is advanced on behalf of the complainant placing reliance upon the verdicts of the Hon'ble High 
Court of Gujarat in Gujarat State Electricity Corporation LTD vs. Bhimrao Aagete (LPA 177 / 2016 dated 
06.03.2018), Kalavatiben Prabhakar Patil and others vs. Managing Director (C/SCA/3189/2020 dated 
17.01.2022) that while deciding a complaint u/s 33A it is not obligatory for the workman to prove that he had 
worked for 240 days. Those rulings in fact do not indicate that the complainant is not at all under obligation to 
substantiate his basic status under the opposite party to justify the case put forth. 


19. Inthe peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and the very casual manner in which it is manned by the 
complainant, the plethora of rulings relied upon by him viz., Hindustan Lever LTD vs. Ram Mohan Roy and 
others (AIR 1973 SC 1156) by the Hon'ble Apex Court, Management of Karur Vysya Bank LTD vs. 
Presiding Officer, Industrial Tribunal (2007 II LLJ 459) by the Hon'ble High Court of Madras, M M 
Narayana vs. KSRTC (AIR 2012 (4) KAR R 518) and Karan Kumar vs. Divisional Controller KSRTC 
(WP 203333/2019 dated 13.07.2023) by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka and Deutsche Lufthansa AG vs. 
Nayan Pahwa & others (2025 INSC 998) by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi are not of any help to the 
complainant as in all those cases non-compliance of the provisions by the respective employers are relating to 
regular employees on its payroll. Among the cases noted above, the case of Karur Vysya Bank LTD, MM 
Narayana and Karan Kumar are related to the actions initiated by the respective employers based on 
misconduct / misdemeanor of the respective regular employees in respect of which approval applications were 
not submitted by the employers. In Hindustan Lever’s case also, the complainants were the regular employees 
of the employer establishment. In principle, the fact situations contained in the afore-quoted ruling do not have 
any application to the case on hand. 


20. Before concluding, it is worthy to pen down that in order to avail the relief provided u/s 33 of the Act, 
firstly the aggrieved party should prove himself to be a workman within the definition of u/s 2(s) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act and there exists employer-employee relationship between the contesting parties. In conclusion of 
the afore-discussion, I find that the complainant has miserably failed in substantiating his own case. The specific 
reason for his so called expulsion from job is the personal vendetta of the then Branch Manager based on a 
flimsy and flippant incident. The opposite party per contra denied and disowned happening of such an incident. 
So much so, the said event being the one within the personal knowledge of the complainant ought to have been 
proved and established by adducing cogent evidence by tendering oral testimony and / or by examining a co- 
employee / witness to the incident. He equally failed in refuting / negating the contentions raised by the opposite 
party that he is only a coolie engaged on need and requirement basis without continuity and frequency and hence 
not governed by any rules and regulations of the bank. So also the complainant further failed in successfully 
controverting the rival contentions of the opposite party that there is no employee-employer relationship between 
himself and the opposite party or that he was not engaged by the latter against a sanctioned post. The deliberate 
refusal, negligence or avoidance to prove and establish a genuine and reliable case by tendering requisite 
evidence has led the complainant to face a total failure in the given case and for an eventual dismissal of the 
complaint. With this view, these points are answered accordingly. 


21. Point No. 5:- In view of the findings on point no. | to 4, it is held that the complainant is not entitled for 
any reliefs sought for in this complaint. 


22. Point no. 6:- In the result the following award is passed. 
AWARD 
The Complaint no. 01/2019 is dismissed.

ORDER 


1. This is a complaint filed by the complainant u/s 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 raising the 
following contentions:- 


The complainant was appointed by the opposite party in the post of MCS / Office Assistant 
(Multipurpose) / Substaff at their Bommalapura branch on 02.12.2010. He submitted application and documents 
and attended interview for selection. Since then he worked continuously in the said branch till the date of his 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 69 


termination / retrenchment / discharge / dismissal of his service on 01.10.2016. As a part of his job, he used to 
open the branch by collecting keys from the Manager, cleaning the office, aiding the customers and the branch in 
various ways. In order to avoid the extension of status and benefits of permanent workman to him, the Opposite 
Party directed the Bommalapura branch to debit his wages as coolie charges to the General ledger account 
without obtaining his signature on the debit vouchers. The officials of the branch took his signature on the 
overleaf of coolie paid debit vouchers along with the signatures of the branch officers while paying wages in 
cash to him. He was the only person doing the work of the office attendant / messenger / sweeper / substaff / 
daily wager / MCS etc on coolie charges. The Opposite Party was not marking attendance register for his work, 
not extended payment register to him, signing debit vouchers for his wages by the officers of the bank and 
receiving amount by them and then paying the amounts to him as wages, debiting the wages paid to him to 
General Charges Account instead of salary paid account / Establishment charges, not issuing appointment orders 
or certificates for the services rendered by him in the bank, refusal to pay wages applicable to messengers / 
housekeeping staff / sub staff / MCS to him, not extending the service benefits applicable to permanent 
workman, taking work from him for years together as Coolie by terming his wages as coolie charges practiced 
by the opposite party are all unfair labour practices under the 5" Schedule of the ID Act 1947. The complainant 
along with other coolie workers of the opposite party bank formed a union called Pragathi Grameena Bank Daily 
Wage Workers Union in 2012 and he was active in the Union activities. The Union filed cases before the Central 
Labour Machinery for getting the benefits for the daily wage workers of the Bank. This has caused annoyance to 
the then management against him. CR 15/2015 is pending before this Tribunal in which the Union raised a 
dispute for regularization of services of the workmen including him. He is directly connected with the said 
dispute raised by the said union. On 01.10.2016, the Branch Manager Mr. Prashanth has asked the complainant 
to work under a contractor Gajamukha Agencies in the Bank or not to come for work. As he was not ready to 
work under the contractor and his services were terminated from 01.10.2016. His services are terminated 
abruptly without any reason and without issuing any notice to him or paying any retrenchment compensation. 
His repeated requests to allow him to do work in the branch were not considered by the Branch Manager. The 
opposite party has not filed any application before the appropriate Government seeking permission to retrench 
him u/s 25 N of the ID Act 1947. Therefore, the retrenchment of his service is illegal, ab-initio void and he is 
deemed to be in the services of the Bank as per sec 25 N(7) of the ID Act. As per the provision of Sec 33 of the 
ID Act, the opposite party cannot alter or change the conditions of his service applicable to him immediately 
before the commencement of the proceedings of C R 15/2015 to his prejudice , during the pendency of CR 
15/2015 before this Tribunal without the expressed permission in writing from the tribunal and also shall not 
discharge / dismiss / terminate / retrench him unless he was paid wages for one month and without making an 
application for approval of the action so taken. The opposite party has not observed any of the provisions of the 
ID Act 1947 and has not filed any application before the Tribunal. The action of the opposite party is against the 
provisions of the ID Act, principles of natural justice, illegal, null and void. The opposite party was paying him 
wages @ Rs. 6500/- per month. The opposite party has not paid any wages to him since the retrenchment of his 
services. Since the opposite party has not filed any application before the Tribunal seeking approval of their 
action, he is entitled for payment of full wages drawn by him every month till the disposal of this case. Since the 
opposite party has not filed any application before the appropriate government for the termination of his services, 
not issued any copy of such application to him nor any notice / notice pay / compensation as required u/s 25 N of 
the ID Act, he is deemed to be in service for the benefits as applicable to him prior to such cessation of his 
service and is entitled for wages as per sec 25N (7) of the ID Act. Due to the illegal cessation of service imposed 
on him by the opposite party, the complainant and his family are suffering economically and socially. Hence this 
complaint for declaring the termination / retrenchment / discharge / dismissal of the complainant from 
01.10.2016 is not in accordance with the provisions of the ID Act 1947, against the principles of natural justice, 
arbitrary, unilateral, ill motivated and illegal and to direct the opposite party to reinstate the complainant with 
full back wages, continuity of service with regularization, ancillary benefits from 01.10.2016 and with cost. 


2. The opposite party at the outset has contended that the complainant has no enforceable cause of action to 
file this complaint and to get any relief. There is no discharge or termination of employment and no Industrial 
Dispute lie under the Act 1947. Ther e is no post of messenger cum sweeper in the Bank. Recruitment and 
appointment of employees in the Regional Rural Banks is governed by the rules framed by the Government of 
India vide notification dated 13.07.2010 called “Regional Rural Banks (Appointment and Promotions of Officers 
and Employees) Rules 2010”. As per the said rules, procedure with regard to Office Attendant (Multipurpose 
Group C employees) are prescribed, the selection process being on the basis of interview to be conducted by a 
Committee. The branches / offices of the bank engage coolies occasionally and intermittently as and when 
necessitated for doing menial works in the branches. In order to meet the exigencies of the work, the opposite 
party bank branches used to engage coolies only for few hours for such menial works like cleaning, sweeping 
and watering and were paid coolie charges proportionately depending upon the number of hours they worked. 
For such menial works in the branches, no condition regarding educational qualification or age is stipulated. 
Depending upon the availability of the person in the locale, the Branch Manager engaged such person on need 
basis for such works. The complainant was also engaged similarly as a coolie intermittently and not 
continuously. As per the Government of India guidelines for appointment of Regular Attendants, the names 


70 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


should be sponsored by the employment exchange and such engagement is also subject to the conditions 
stipulated in regard to educational qualification, age etc. While engaging the coolies, no educational 
qualifications or age were looked into and whoever is available would be engaged. They are not governed by any 
rules and regulation of the bank and there is no employee employer relationship as they have not been engaged 
by the bank against the post. It is the settled position in law that a person engaged intermittently on daily wages 
will not have the right to be absorbed for any post. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Secretary, State of 
Karnataka vs. Uma Devi have laid down the law relating to regularization / permanency claims of casual 
employees. In Union of India vs. A S_ Pillai also the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that daily wager / part time 
workers not engaged in any regular cadres or any sanctioned post are not entitled for absorption. The contention 
of the complainant that he was appointed by the opposite party at their Bommalapura branch on 02.12.2010 by 
taking application form etc. is denied. The Branch Manager has no power to recruit / appoint any employee. The 
complainant was engaged only occasionally to attend to menial / urgent works and not continuously. Since the 
complainant was not recruited / appointed by the opposite party anytime, his termination / dismissal / 
retrenchment on 01.10.2016 did not arise. Consequently, question of issuing notice to him, payment of 
retrenchment compensation, payment of wages of one month, filing of application before the Tribunal before or 
during the pendency of CR 15/2015 and seeking permission u/s 25N of the Act does not arise. Under the 
circumstances, sec 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act has no application in his case. He was never engaged for 
attending the regular functions of substaff. He was paid wages for the occasional / casual works he was engaged 
to. The Branch Managers are not authorized to issue any certificates and question of issuing certificates to him 
does not arise as he was not continuously engaged in the opposite party bank and nor was empanelled in the 
daily wagers’ list. The complainant has not been appointed in the payrolls of the opposite party at any time. 
Since he has not been appointed in the opposite party bank, question of marking in the attendance register, 
extending payment registered to him, debiting the payment made to him to salary account, issuing appointment 
orders, issuing certificates and denying benefits etc. did not arise. Hence the allegation of unfair labour practice 
on the part of the opposite party is untenable. The contention of the complainant that his involvement in the 
union activities and filing of Industrial Dispute by the said union for getting benefits to the daily wage workers 
has caused anger to the opposite party is a figment of his imagination and hence denied. The complainant was 
not working in the opposite party bank on continuous basis and was engaged occasionally, casually for menial 
and urgent requirements. His contention that he was being paid wages @ Rs. 6500/- is denied. His contentions 
that he was deemed to be in service and entitled for benefits are untenable and baseless. The complainant has not 
undergone any process of recruitment and is not entitled for recruitment for appointment in the opposite party 
bank or for reinstatement or other ancillary benefits as claimed by him. For all these reasons, the opposite party 
has prayed for rejection of the complaint. 


3. | From the above rival pleadings, following points arise for consideration:- 
1, Whether the complaint is legally and factually maintainable? 


2. Whether the Complainant is proved to have been working continuously in the opposite party 
establishment since 02.12.2010? 


3. Whether the complainant is proved to have been discharged / terminated / retrenched / dismissed 
from service as contended by him? 


4. Whether the alleged contravention of the provision of sec 33 of the ID Act is proved by the 
complainant? 


5. Whether the complainant is entitled to get reinstatement to the service with full back wages, 
continuity of service and ancillary benefits from 01.10.2016 as prayed for? 


6. What is the proper Order and Award to be passed in this complaint case? 


4. The complainant has got himself examined in chief as CW1 and Ex Cl is seen marked. When the stage 
came for his cross-examination, the Authorized Representative of the complainant is seen to have submitted that 
the affidavit filed by the complainant on 16.10.2019 in lieu of his examination in chief to be discarded and the 
matter be directly heard. Accordingly, that part of the oral and documentary evidence tendered by the 
complainant stood struck off from record. In effect, there is no evidence on the part of the complainant. 


5. Heard the oral and written arguments submitted from both sides. 


6. Points no. 1 to 4:- Since all these points are closely integrated and inter-twined, all these points are 
discussed together. Alleging contravention of the provisions of sec 33 of the ID Act 1947, the complainant filed 
the instant complaint u/s 33A of the Act on the factual averment that the opposite party has not filed any 
application before this Tribunal seeking permission for retrenching / terminating / dismissing him on 01.10.2016 
and not filing any application for approval of their said action. The complainant’s case is that he was appointed 
by the opposite party bank at their Bommalapura branch on 02.12.2010 on submission of application and 
subjecting him for interview and on obtaining documents from him. He claims that since then he has worked 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 71 


continuously in the said branch on all working days. It is his further case that to his surprise, without giving any 
prior notice or without assigning any reason, he was asked on 01.10.2016 not to come for work and his services 
are terminated. The complainant inter alia pleaded that he is an active member in a Union under the name and 
style Pragathi Grameena Bank Daily Wage Workers Union formed between himself with other coolie workers of 
the opposite party bank. The said union has raised a dispute for regularization of the service of the complainant 
and other similarly placed coolie before the Central Government Machinery and the same is registered and 
pending before this Tribunal as CR 15/2015. It is the case of the complainant that he is directly connected with 
the said dispute raised by the Union pending before this Tribunal. The disengagement of job on 01.10.2016 
according to the complainant tantamounts to contravention of the provisions of sec 33 of the ID Act as according 
to him it happened when the industrial dispute raised by the union for and on behalf of him and the other coolie 
workers was pending adjudication. This gave way for filing this complaint u/s 33A of the ID Act. 


7. Oral and written arguments are advanced on behalf of the complainant narrating all these events by his 
authorized representative. 


8. The learned counsel for the opposite party per contra put forth his rival submission that the complainant has 
never ever rendered any continuous service in the opposite party bank. Instead the bank was in the practice of 
engaging persons from the locale for attending menial job like sweeping, cleaning and watering when the regular 
employees are absent or proceed on leave and such persons were paid coolie charges for the same. According to 
the opposite party, the complainant was also so casually engaged depending on the requirement of the branch as 
a coolie for doing menial works and such works carried out by him was not regular in nature, but only on need 
basis. To put it differently, according to the opposite party the engagement of the complainant was not 
continuous and it was only intermittent. 


9. Ofcourse, the event of non-engagement for work said to have happened on 01.10.2016 is apparently during 
the pendency of CR 15/2015. However the complainant did not prefer to bring home any proof that he was in 
service in the opposite party bank even on the previous day or anytime there-before in a constant and continuous 
stretch so as to establish the retrenchment / dismissal / discharge / termination alleged in the complaint. Here it is 
contextually profitable to quote Sec 33 of the Act: 


33. [ Conditions of service, etc., to remain unchanged under certain circumstances during pendency of 
proceedings. ] 


(1)During the pendency of any conciliation proceeding before a conciliation officer or a Board or of any 
proceeding before ][an arbitrator or] [a Labour Court or Tribunal or National Tribunal in respect of an 
industrial dispute, no employer shall- (a)in regard to any matter connected with the dispute, alter, to the 
prejudice of the workmen concerned in such dispute, the conditions of service applicable to them immediately 
before the commencement of such proceeding; or (b)for any misconduct connected with the dispute, discharge 
or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, any workmen concerned in such dispute, ave with the express 
permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending.(2)During the pendency of any 
such proceeding in respect of an industrial dispute, the employer may, in accordance with the standing orders 
applicable to a workman concerned in such dispute ] [or, where there are no such standing orders, in 
accordance with the terms of the contract, whether express or implied, between him and the workman] (a){ 
alter, in regard to any matter not connected with the dispute, the conditions of service applicable to that 
workman immediately before the commencement of such proceeding; or (b) for any misconduct not connected 
with the dispute, discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, that workman: Provided that no such 
workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one month and an application 
has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending for approval of the 
action taken by the employer. (3)Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (2), no employer shall, 
during the pendency of any such proceeding in respect of an industrial dispute, take any action against any 
protected workman concerned in such dispute (a) by altering, to the prejudice of such protected workman, the 
conditions of service applicable to him immediately before the commencement of such proceedings; or (b) by 
discharging or punishing, whether by dismissal or otherwise, such protected workman, save with the express 
permission in writing of the authority before which the proceeding is pending. Explanation:-For the purposes 
of this sub-section, a "protected workman ", in relation to an establishment, means a workman who, being] [a 
member of the executive or other office bearer] [of a registered trade union connected with the establishment, 
is recognised as such in accordance with rules made in this behalf.(4)In every establishment, the number of 
workmen to be recognised as protected workmen for the purposes of sub-section (3) shall be one per cent. of 
the total number of workmen employed therein subject to a minimum number of five protected workmen and a 
maximum number of one hundred protected workmen and for the aforesaid purpose, the appropriate 
Government may make rules providing for the distribution of such protected workmen among various trade 
unions, if any, connected with the establishment and the manner in which the workmen may be chosen and 
recognised as protected workmen.(5)Where an employer makes an application to a conciliation officer, Board, 
] [an arbitrator, a] [Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal under the proviso to sub-section (2) for 
approval of the action taken by him, the authority concerned shall, without delay, hear such application and 


12 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


pass, ] [within a period of three months from the date of receipt of such application] [ Substituted by Act 46_of 
1982, Section 17, for " as expeditiously as possible" (w.e.f. 21.8.1984).][, such order in relation thereto as it 
deems fit:]. ][Provided that where any such authority considers it necessary or expedient so to do, it may, for 
reasons to be recorded in writing, extend such period by such further period as it may think fit: Provided 
further that no proceedings before any such authority shall lapse merely on the ground that any period 
specified in this sub-section had expired without such proceedings being completed. ] 


10. Of course by enacting sec 33, the legislature wanted to ensure a fair and satisfactory enquiry of the 
industrial dispute undisturbed by any action on the part of the employer or the employee likely to create fresh 
cause for disharmony between them. The legislature visualized that during the pendency of the industrial dispute 
status quo should be maintained and no further element of discord should be introduced between the employer 
and the employee. The objective of the provision of sec 33 is to put a ban on the prerogative of the employer in 
altering the service condition of the employee pending enquiry of the industrial dispute raised by them. The 
primary principle is that if an Industrial Dispute is raised by a group of workmen acting on their own through 
their union, the general conclusion is that the all those who sponsored the dispute are concerned in it. However 
the very factum of raising an Industrial Dispute and pendency of such a dispute in a court of law by an individual 
employee or a group of employees by itself does not lead to the inference that such an individual who alleges 
retrenchment from services was a workman in continuous service under the employer, unless proved by concrete 
evidence. Indeed, Sec 33A stands to the rescue of a workman who alleges alteration or cessation of service by 
the employer during the pendency of an Industrial Dispute. A regular workman / employee or a casual employee 
on a continuing basis under an employer who files a complaint u/s 33A certainly stands on a different footing 
than the one who claims continuity of service as a casual labourer and whose claim is not accepted by the 
employer. 


11. The case on hand portrays the scenario the employer disowns and denies the complainant as its regular 
daily wager. The alleged retrenchment of service dated 01.10.2016 averred by the complainant is not accepted or 
recognized by the Oppose Party in the given case. The definite stand of the opposite party is that the complainant 
had been engaged very occasionally and intermittently on need basis to attend menial works like sweeping, 
cleaning etc. without touching the routine works in the office. The complainant per contra very particularly 
pleaded that apart from cleaning in and around the bank office, he was entrusted with the task of assisting 
customers in making challans for cash / cheque, deposits taking and keeping cash in double lock, writing 
registers, collecting cash from other banks from the cheques drawn on them, printing passbooks, deposit receipts, 
writing loan papers, making deposit mobilization, bundling payment slips and day book and such so many tasks. 
However according to the opposite party all the above works are the routine tasks of the regular employees and 
not of such casual workers engaged for attending menial jobs. Thus the factual pleadings of the complainant 
indicate that his engagement in the opposite party bank was not to attend menial labour alone but higher tasks as 
well, as mentioned above. It is while attending such highly responsible tasks in his so called status as MCS / 
Office assistant (multipurpose) / sub-staff at the Bomallapura branch of the opposite party continuously since 
02.10.2010 that the opposite party has terminated / retrenched his services on 01.10.2016. This factum also the 
opposite party has emphatically opposed and disputed. According to the opposite party, no such retrenchment or 
termination has ever occurred nor was there any occasion for that as the bank had not engaged the complainant 
in such a position at all in work continuously. In this factual background it is the primary duty of the complainant 
to substantiate that his very entry in the bank was on 02.12.2010 and he continued to perform services in the 
opposite party bank without any break till 01.10.2016. The complainant is equally obliged to prove that he was 
disengaged from a continuous service on 01.10.2016. Inability to offer menial job on a particular date when there 
was no requirement to engage a casual labourer to attend such work pleaded by the opposite party does oblige 
the complainant to substantiate his specific case by adducing reliable and concrete material evidence establishing 
all the aspects pleaded by him in the complaint. The mere pleading raised by him regarding the prevalence / 
pendency of an Industrial Dispute and the so called termination or retrenchment of services on 01.10.2016 
without bringing home any iota of evidence substantiating the above plea does not bind this Tribunal to accept 
the case set forth by him as gospel truth and to draw a finding against the opposite party. 


12. Itis the settled position of law that u/s 33A of the Industrial Dispute Act, the complainant carries the initial 
burden / onus to prove that the employer contravened sec 33 of the Act and such contravention occurred during 
the pendency of a dispute, by presenting the facts supported by evidence. Once the complainant discharges his 
initial burden to establish that he is an employee in continuous service within the parameters of sec 33 of the Act 
and such contravention occurred as pleaded and proved, the employer must then justify their actions especially 
concerning alleged dismissal / retrenchment / termination, often leading to the tribunal deciding if the action was 
fair and just like any other Industrial Dispute. 


13. Here in the given case, the one and only aspect accepted and admitted by the opposite party is the pendency 
of CR 15/2015 raised by the Daily Workers Union. That by itself does not discharge the onus of proof cast on the 
complainant to prima facie establish its case. The alleged contravention of service conditions or an illegal 
cessation of the service of an employee by the employer is not an aspect to be simply inferred by the Tribunal 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 73 


out of nothing but to be very precisely, meticulously and scrupulously proved and established by the aggrieved 
complainant. 


14. Sec 33A is designed to provide an instant remedy to a workman aggrieved by the contravention of sec 33 
by filing a complaint before adjudicatory authorities or conciliatory authorities. It is trite that where such a 
complaint is made to an adjudicatory authority viz. Labour Court / Tribunal, it will adjudicate upon the dispute 
as if it is a dispute referred to or pending before it, so that the workman is saved of the botheration of moving the 
Government for referring this dispute for adjudication. 


15. The basic question to be considered by this Tribunal in the complaint on hand u/s 33A is whether there has 
been a contravention by the employer of the provisions of sec 33 and in the event it is found that there has been a 
contravention of the provisions, then to embark upon the exercise to adjudicate about the matter so complained 
of in the complaint on its merit. No written order of termination / retrenchment is produced by the complainant to 
justify his pleadings. Of course, he averred in the complaint that the termination issued by the opposite party was 
only oral. If that be so, it should be proved by the complainant that he was in continuous service under the 
opposite party and was subjected for a termination / retrenchment on an oral order by mounting the witness box. 
Going by the proceedings underwent in the given case, it is clear that once the statement of objection is filed by 
the opposite party, the matter was posted for evidence of the complainant. Though initially the complainant has 
got himself examined in chief as CW1 and Ex Cl is seen marked, when the stage came for his cross- 
examination, the Authorized Representative of the complainant is seen to have submitted that the affidavit filed 
by the complainant on 16.10.2019 in lieu of his examination in chief is to be discarded and the matter be directly 
heard. Accordingly, that part of the oral and documentary evidence tendered by the complainant stood struck off 
from record. In effect, there is no evidence on the part of the complainant. In fact, as per law, before giving any 
relief to the aggrieved employee under the section, the authority viz., this Tribunal has first to determine that the 
employee was continuously working under the employer and the latter had surreptitiously kicked out him from 
the job without complying with the mandate u/s 33 of the Act. Hence a contravention of sec 33 is the foundation 
for exercise of the power u/s 33A of the Act. As already observed and as rightly pointed out by the learned 
counsel for the opposite party, no reliable proof / evidence is brought on record by the complainant to 
substantiate that there is contravention of provisions of sec 33 of the Act from the side of the opposite party. 


16. In the event if the alleged factum of infraction from the provision of sec 33 is established, the matter has to 
be very meticulously adjudicated on merit to examine whether the complainant is entitled to get an order of 
reinstatement. It is trite that even when contravention of sec 33 is established, that does not automatically lead to 
an order for reinstatement. So, at large, the complainant is at the task to prove and establish the primary elements 
viz., his status as a daily wage employee under the opposite party coupled with contravention of the provisions of 
sec 33 by the latter and then his eventual right to get reinstatement to service with equivalent benefits. 
Determination of all these issues by the legal forum could be possible only when reliable evidence is adduced by 
the complainant by offering himself for searching cross examination by the opposite party in a full-fledged trial. 
It is trite that the initial burden lies on the employee to prove that he falls under the definition of a “workman” 
under the Industrial Dispute Act. If the employee presents a strong prima facie case, the management must then 
provide evidence to rebut it. Of course, the evidence to be adduced by the person claiming to be an employee 
must be substantial, often a preponderance of evidence depending on the claim. It is no longer res-integra that the 
burden of proving the employer-employee relationship primarily rest upon the person who asserts its existence. 
In a situation where a person asserts to be an employee of the management which the management denies, the 
duty primarily rests upon the person so asserting to give positive evidence in his favour and discharge his initial 
burden. At the risk of repetition I say, once such a person has given such a positive evidence in his favour, only 
then the burden would shift on the management to give evidence to counter such claims, because it is always 
possible to prove positive facts than a negative. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Workman of Nilgiri Co-Op 
Mkt Society LTD vs. State of Tamil Nadu (AIR 2004 SC 1639) held that it is a well settled principle of law 
that the person who is setting up a plea of existence of relationship of employer and employee, the burden would 
be upon him. Similar view is adopted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Bank of Baroda vs. Ghemarabhai 
Harijibhai Rabari (2005 (10) SCC 792). The complainant herein kept aloof from trial feeling shy of an 
intensive quiz in the witness box. Probably, the complainant might have been misled, misguided or mal-advised 
not to mount the witness box so as to avoid probable inconvenience of a grilling cross-examination. The net 
result of such willful avoidance of requisite procedure by the complainant either by himself or as instilled upon 
him is complete failure of the case projected by him. 


17. Extensive argument is advanced on behalf of the complainant with the aid of plethora of legal authorities 
canvassing for a favorable order of reinstatement with full back wages, continuity of service with regularization 
and ancillary benefits from 01.10.2016. As could be heard from Learned Counsel for the opposite party, all these 
wider reliefs sought for by the complainant are the main reliefs claimed in the said case CR 15/2015. By 
consciously avoiding to give oral or documentary evidence in this case, what is craved for on behalf of the 
complainant is to grant the above reliefs even without facing a trial. Granting such reliefs in his favour without 
providing / supplementing any sort of evidentiary support would tantamount to prejudging the issue raised in the 


74 


THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Industrial Dispute case CR 15/2015 in a very shortcut method. 


18. Argument is advanced on behalf of the complainant placing reliance upon the verdicts of the Hon'ble High 
Court of Gujarat in Gujarat State Electricity Corporation LTD vs. Bhimrao Aagete (LPA 177 / 2016 dated 
06.03.2018), Kalavatiben Prabhakar Patil and others vs. Managing Director (C/SCA/3189/2020 dated 
17.01.2022) that while deciding a complaint u/s 33A it is not obligatory for the workman to prove that he had 
worked for 240 days. Those rulings in fact do not indicate that the complainant is not at all under obligation to 
substantiate his basic status under the opposite party to justify the case put forth. 


19. In the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and the very casual manner in which it is manned by the 
complainant, the plethora of rulings relied upon by him viz., Hindustan Lever LTD vs. Ram Mohan Roy and 
others (AIR 1973 SC 1156) by the Hon'ble Apex Court, Management of Karur Vysya Bank LTD vs. 
Presiding Officer, Industrial Tribunal (2007 II LLJ 459) by the Hon'ble High Court of Madras, M M 
Narayana vs. KSRTC (AIR 2012 (4) KAR R 518) and Karan Kumar vs. Divisional Controller KSRTC 
(WP 203333/2019 dated 13.07.2023) by the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka and Deutsche Lufthansa AG vs. 
Nayan Pahwa & others (2025 INSC 998) by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi are not of any help to the 
complainant as in all those cases non-compliance of the provisions by the respective employers are relating to 
regular employees on its payroll. Among the cases noted above, the case of Karur Vysya Bank LTD, MM 
Narayana and Karan Kumar are related to the actions initiated by the respective employers based on 
misconduct / misdemeanor of the respective regular employees in respect of which approval applications were 
not submitted by the employers. In Hindustan Lever’s case also, the complainants were the regular employees 
of the employer establishment. In principle, the fact situations contained in the afore-quoted ruling do not have 
any application to the case on hand. 


20. Before concluding, it is worthy to pen down that in order to avail the relief provided u/s 33 of the Act, 
firstly the aggrieved party should prove himself to be a workman within the definition of u/s 2(s) of the Industrial 
Dispute Act and there exists employer-employee relationship between the contesting parties. In conclusion of the 
afore-discussion, I find that the complainant has miserably failed in substantiating his own case. He equally 
failed in refuting / negating the contentions raised by the opposite party that he is only a coolie engaged on need 
and requirement basis without continuity and frequency and hence not governed by any rules and regulations of 
the bank. So also the complainant further failed in successfully controverting the rival contentions of the 
opposite party that there is no employee-employer relationship between himself and the opposite party or that he 
was not engaged by the latter against a sanctioned post. The deliberate refusal, negligence or avoidance to prove 
and establish a genuine and reliable case by tendering requisite evidence has led the complainant to face a total 
failure in the given case and for an eventual dismissal of the complaint. With this view, these points are 
answered accordingly. 


21. Point No. 5:- In view of the findings on point no. | to 4, it is held that the complainant is not entitled for 
any reliefs sought for in this complaint. 


22. Point no. 6:- In the result the following award is passed. 
AWARD 
The Complaint no. 03/2019 is dismissed.
