AWARD 


The Government of India in the Ministry of Labour &Employment in exercising its power conferred under 
clause (d) of sub-section (1) and sub-section (2-A) of Section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (14 of 1947) 
have referred a dispute between the Management of UCO Bank, Begedia Branch and allegedly its workmen vide 
letter No. L-12012/06/2017 — IR(B-II), dated 20.03.2017 for its adjudication and the schedule of the reference is as 
follows:- 


“Whether the action of the management of UCO Bank, Bagedia Branch, Dist. Angul, Odisha in terminating 
Smt. Kalpana Pradhan w.e.f. 19.01.2016 without assigning any reason and without following the provisions 
of LD. Act, 1947 is legal & justified? If not, to what relief the workman is entitled to?” 


2: The case of the 2™ party-work woman as per her statement of claim is as follows:- 


That, her husband late Saudagar Pradhan was a sub-staff of the Bagadia Branch of UCO Bank and he died on 
24.03.2010. Thereafter she was employed as a daily labourer since 26.04.2010 and she was assured for her regular 
employment. She was discharging her duties continuously in the Bank but on 19.01.2016, the Branch Manager of 


102 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Bagadia branch of UCO Bank had terminated her services without any prior notice resulting financial loss and mental 
agony. Thereafter she approached the A.L.C.(Central), Angul and on failure of conciliation the matter was referred to 
as a reference to this Tribunal for adjudication. The action of the Management, Branch Manager, UCO Bank is highly 
illegal and arbitrary as it had been terminated her services without any notice or retrenchment benefit. 


A prayer has been made to pass an award declaring her retrenchment by the Management of UCO Bank as 
null and void with a direction to reappoint her with full back wages. 


3. The 1“ Party-Management through the Branch Manager, UCO Bank, Bagadia Branch has appeared and filed 
written statement. 


4. The case of the 17 Party-Management as per its written statement is as follows:- 


That, the 2" party is not a “workman” of the management-Bank and there was no “employer and employee” 
relationship existed between the Management with the 2™ Party-work-woman at any point of time, so there is no 
industrial dispute exists in this case. The 2™ party is not a workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, so the present reference is bad in law. The services of the 2" party-work-woman Smt. 
Kalpana Pradhan was availed in the Bank as occasionally on as and when basis so it cannot be decided how many 
days she had worked in the Bank. Moreover, the Bank has never issued any appointment letter or termination letter to 
the workwoman, so the compliance of Section 25-F of the ID. Act does not arise in this case. She had never 
completed continuous service in the Bank for more than 240 days in a year preceding to her termination. The 27 party 
workwoman after the death of her husband had approached the Branch Manager of the Bagadia Branch of UCO Bank 
for providing her some part time miscellaneous work and the Branch Manager on humanitarian ground offered her 
some miscellaneous work as and when required. The 2™ party-work-woman was not an employee of the Bank so she 
had not marked her presence in the attendance register and she had never worked continuously in any year of her 
contractual engagement continuously and uninterruptedly. The Management-Bank is not under any obligation to 
serve any notice and no illegal & arbitrary action had been taken by the Management against her. 


A prayer has been made by the 1‘ Party-Management to dismiss __ the claim of the 2™ party-work-woman as 
she is not entitled for any __ relief. 


5. The 21 party-workman has filed rejoinder to the written statement filed by the 17 Party-Management 
denying all the averments made by the 17 Party-Management. 


6. On the basis of the pleadings of both the parties following issues _ are framed. 
ISSUES 
i) Whether the reference is maintainable? 


ii) Whether any action of the management of UCO Bank, Bagadia Branch, Dist. Angul, Odisha in terminating 
Smt. Kalpana Pradhan w.e.f. 19.01.2016 without assigning any reason and without following the provisions 
of I.D. Act, 1947 is legal & Justified? 


iii) Ifnot, to what relief the workman is entitled to? 


7. The 2™ party-workman has examined only one witness. She is the workwoman herself Kalpana Pradhan as 
W.W.-1 and she has proved _ the following documents which are marked as hereunder:- 


Ext.-1 — Copy of the application filed by the applicant before the A.L.C©, Angul. 

Ext.-2 — Copy of the Statement of claim. 

Ext.-3 — Copy of representation to the Management by the applicant on dated 03.02.2016. 

Ext.-4 — Copy of the request letter to the concerned B.M., UCO Bank, Bagadia Branch, Angul. 

Ext.-5 Series — Copies of the payment receipts. 

Ext.-6 — Copy of the death certificate of Late Soudagar Pradhan husband _ of the 27 Party-workman. 

Ext.-7 — Copy of the HSC pass Certificate issued by the BSE, Odisha, Cuttack in favour of the 2"! Party-Workman. 
Ext.-8 series — Copies of the Debit vouchers. 

Ext.-9 series — Copies of the vouchers entry register containing entries from January, 2010 to January, 2016, 


8. On the other-hand the 1“ Party-Management has examined only one witness. He is Ashish Kumar Behera 
Asst. Manager, UCO Bank, Bagadia Branch of Angul. 


9: In course of his evidence he has proved the following documents which are marked as :- 


[भाग --खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 103 


Ext.-A — Copy of the representation of the work-woman dated 04.05.2011 for placement under rehabilitation. 


FINDINGS 
ISSUE NO. 1 & I 
10. Both the issues are taken up together for the sake of convenience. 
11. At the outset of discussions it is required to mention here that it is an admitted fact that late Saudagar 


Pradhan, husband of the 21 party-work-work-woman was a sub-staff of the Management-Bank at Bagadia Branch 
and he died on 24.04.2010. Further it is also admitted fact that after the death of late Saudagar Pradhan his wife 2" 
party workwoman was engaged by the Management-Bank occasionally as and when basis. 


12. It is the case of the 2" Party-workman that after the death of late Saudagar Pradhan, his wife Kalpana 
Pradhan was employed as a daily labourer since 26.04.2010 till 19.01.2016. However, the 1“ Party-Management has 
denied that the 2™ party-work-woman was engaged on daily wage basis regularly. 


13. Now in the light of the above discussions, the Tribunal thinks it proper to discuss the oral and documentary 
evidence available in the record. 


14. The most competent witness in this case is W.W.-1. Smt. Kalpana Pradhan who has fully supported her case 
in the evidence. She has categorically deposed that she was employed as a daily 1 abourer with effect from 
26.04.2010 on post of her husband under the Management and she performed her duty continuously and 
uninterruptedly under the 17 Party-Management till the date of her illegal termination. She has also stated 
that during her service tenure her work was fixed from 9.30 A.M. till closure of the Bank and she was paid monthly 
salary by the Management on the first week of the subsequent month by signing on cash vouchers on the head 
of wage of casual labourers. She has also stated that while receiving payments of monthly wages she had signed _at 
the back side of the cash voucher in respect of token of receipt of her wages. She has also stated that after the death of 
her husband she was allowed by the Bank authority to work in place of her husband and she — was discharging all the 
duties what her husband was doing. She has further stated that she had discharged her duties by sorting of daily 
vouchers by entering total number of vouchers in the register provided by the Bank authority on date-wise and 
supplied necessary forms to the customers. She has also stated that she had discharged her duties on the direction 
of the Bank authority. She has further stated that she had continuously discharging her duties uninterruptedly and 
performed her duty from 26.04.2010 till 19.01.2016 under the 17 Party-Management __ but she had been terminated 
from the services without assigning any reason and without giving any prior notice, so she was illegally terminated 
from her services. She has also deposed that she had raised _ the dispute before the labour authorities and on failure 


of the conciliation proceeding the present reference arose. She has proved the documents which are marked as 
Ext.-1 to Ext.-9. 
In the cross examination she has stated that after the death of her husband she was paid around Rs. 


35,000/- towards the death benefit of her husband. She has also deposed that on 04.05.2011 she has made 
representation to the Zonal Manager, Sambalpur for her rehabilitation appointment as she was working for a long 
period on daily wage basis. She has also deposed that she used to sign on each voucher when salary was paid to 
her and she had worked in the same capacity in the branch when her husband was alive. She has also —_— deposed that 
she was not engaged in the branch in January 2010 to 25.04.2010. She has also deposed that she had collected the 
documents on the instruction of the Branch Manager. She has denied the fact that the assertions made in Para-6, 7 
and 8 of the affidavit evidence were baseless and false and the assertions made in Para-5, 6, 7, 8,9, 10, 11, 12, 15, 
16, 18 and 19 in the affidavit evidence were —_ beyond the pleadings. She has denied the suggestion that she was not 
a workman of the 17 Party-management and there was no employee and employer relationship between the 
Management and her. 


15. The Management witness No. | Sri Asish Kumar Behera who is the Assistant Manager of UCO Bank, 
Bagadia Branch has deposed that _ the services of the 2" party-workwoman Smt. Kalpana Prahan was _ availed by 
the Bank occasionally on as and when basis and it cannot be _ said that that how many days she had worked in the 
branch and how many days she had worked for other organization. He has also deposed that Smt. Kalpana Pradhan 
was not an employee of the Bank and neither any appointment letter nor termination letter was issued to her. 
He has further stated that the 27 party-work-woman had never made any application for her appointment or 
engagement in the Bank and the documents which are marked a Ext.-1, 2 3 & 4 are forged and created document for 
the purpose of this case. That the 2" party-woman had never rendered continuous service in the Bank for 240 days in 
any calendar year preceding of her termination, so the provisions of Section- 25 of the I.D. Act is not 
applicable. He has further deposed that —_ on the death of husband of the 2™ party-workwoman, she approached the 
Branch Manager and considering her request she was offered some miscellaneous job as and when required. He has 
also deposed that the disputant workwoman had never worked continuously and —_uninterruptedly for 240 days 
preceding to the date of her alleged termination. He has also stated that the disputant work-woman had submitted a 
representation on 04.05.2011 to the Zonal Manager, Sambalpur for her placement on the ground that she was doing 
some __ part time work in the branch since 11.06.2010. He had also stated that the Management is not under any 


104 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


obligation to serve any notice and there is no illegal and arbitrary action against the 27 party workwoman. He 
has proved the photocopy of the representation of the workwoman dated 04.05.2011 which is marked as Ext.-A. 


In the cross examination he has deposed that he has no direct knowledge about engagement and 
disengagement of the workwoman at the Bagadia Branch. He has further stated that after going through the 
written statement filed in this case and the other documents I am deposing before this Tribunal. He has also deposed 
that he had no knowledge and he had not gone through the documents showing how many days the workwoman had 
worked for any other organization. He has also deposed that on the basis of earlier affidavit filed by the 
Management he can say Ext.-1 to Ex.-4 are forged and created for the purpose of this case. He has also deposed that 
nothing has been mentioned in the written statement of the Management regarding letter of the representation of 
the workman dated 04.05.2011. He has denied the suggestion that Smt. Kalpana Pradhan was not working since 
26.04.2010 to 18.01.2016. 


16. Now coming to the documentary evidence of the work-woman it appears that Ext.-4 is a request letter 
submitted to the Branch Manager, Bagadia Branch of UCO Bank, Angul for considering her case as she was 
working as a daily wager employed since 2010 after death of her husband. Further Ext.-5 series are the vouchers 
containing 41 sheets showing payment of coolie charges and on the back of it the name of the work-woman 
Smt. Kalpana Pradhan was mentioned. Ext.-8 series are the debit vouchers for the period 2011, 2012 showing 
payment and on the back of the said debit vouchers there is signature of the work-woman Smt. Kalpana Pradhan 
showing payment in cash. Ext.-9 series are the copies of the vouchers entry register containing entries from 
January, 2010 to January, 2016. However, the Management has proved the representation of the work- 
workman Smt. Kalpana Pradhan which is Ext.-A for her placement under the rehabilitation in which it has been 
mentioned that she was doing some job as part time in banking hours since 11.06.2010. 


17. At this stage, it is important to mention here that the definition of workman has been defined U/s 2(s) of 
the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 (14 of 1947) which reads as follows:- 


“workman” means any person (including an apprentice) employed in any industry to do any manual, 
unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the 
terms of employment be express or implied, and for the purposes of any proceeding under this 
Act in relation to an industrial dispute, includes any such __ person who has been dismissed, discharged 
or retrenched in connection with, or as a consequence of, that dispute, or whose dismissal, 
discharge or retrenchment has led to that dispute, but does not include any such person- 


(i) who is subject to the Air Force Act, 1950 (45 of 1950), or the Army Act, 1950 (46 of 1950), or 
the Navy Act, 1957 (62 of 1957); or 


(ii) who is employed in the police service or as an officer or other employee of a person, or 
(iii) who is employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity, or 


(iv) who, being employed in a supervisory capacity, draws wages exceeding (ten thousand rupees) 
per mensem or exercises, either by the nature of the duties attached to the office or by reason of the 
powers vested in him, functions mainly of a managerial nature 


18. It is relevant to mention here that the Hon’ble Supreme Court in a case as reported in 2011 LAB. 1. C. 
2799 (S.C) has been pleased to observe as follows:- 


“14. It is apposite to observe that the definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full-time and part-time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing 
in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only a person employed on 
regular basis or a person employed for doing whole-time job is a workman and the one employed 
on temporary, part-time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing 
duty for fixed hours is not a workman. 


15. | Whenever an employer challenges the maintainability ground that the employee is not a 
workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act, what the Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal is 
required to consider is whether the person is employed in an industry for hire or reward for 
doing manual, unskilled, skilled, operational, technical or clerical work in an industry. Once the test 
of employment for hire or reward for doing the specified type of work is satisfied, | the employee 
would fall within the definition of “workman”. 


19. Now in this case there is a consistent oral and documentary evidence on behalf of the 27 party-workman 
that she was working as a daily wage employee in the Bagadia Branch of UCO Bank at Angul since 
26.04.2010 after death of her husband. Moreover Ext.-5 series and Ext.-8 series show payment of wages to the 
work-woman and receiving of the same after making endorsement on the back side of [16 payment vouchers as 
well as debit vouchers. Further, it is the admission on behalf of the Management that the services of the 2™ party- 
workwoman Smt. Kalpana Pradhan was availed by the Bank occasionally as and when basis. 


20. In view of the above discussions and in view of the decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court as 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 105 


discussed (supra) the Tribunal finds and holds that the concerned workman Smt. Kalpana Pradhan was a 
work-woman under section 2(s) of the I.D. Act and there is an industrial dispute. 


21. At this stage, it is required to mention here that the there is consistent oral and documentary evidence of 
the W.W.-1 Smt. Kalpana Pradhan that she had worked under the 1% Party-Management 
since 26.04.2010 to 19.01.2016 which is more than the 240 days in a calendar year. However, the M.W.-1 in his 
evidence has denied that the 27 party-workwoman had discharged her duties in the Bank continuously for 240 
days in a calendar year. 


22. In this regard it is relevant to mention here that the Ext.-5, shows that 2™ Party-workwoman Smt. 
Kalpana Pradhan had received her payment through vouchers by the 1“ Party-Management for the period 2011- 
2012 and onwards. Further Ext.-8 also shows that she had been paid through debit vouchers for the period 
2011-2012 and there-after the payment made through vouchers. Ext.-5 & Ext.-8 establishes the fact that the 2™ 
party work-woman was working under the 17 Party-Management otherwise why the 1 Party-Management 
had made payment to her through vouchers. After — making calculations of the period it appears that the 2™ party- 
workwoman Smt. Kalpana Pradhan had worked for more than 240 days in a calendar year. 


23. Further when the 27 party-workwoman has raised that she had worked for 240 days in a calendar 
year then the burden of proof 65 on the Management to disprove that she had not worked for more than 
240 days in any calendar year. However, the Management has proved Ext.-A which is a representation 
submitted by the workman in which it has been categorically mentioned that she had been working in the 
Bagadia branch of UCO Bank, Angul since 10.06.2010. 


24. In view of the above discussions the Tribunal finds and holds that the 27 party-work woman Smt. 
Kalpana Pradhan had worked under the 1% Party-Management-Bank for more than 240 days in each 
and every calendar year and she had been terminated from __ service with effect from 19.10.2016. 


25. It is relevant to mention here that the word retrenchment has been defined U/s. 2(00) of the I.D. Act, the 
definition of Continuous service has been mentioned u/s 25-B of I.D. Act and the Condition Precedent to 
Retrenchment have been mentioned U/s 25-F of I.D. Act. 


Section 2(00) of the I.D. Act reads as follows:- 


Section 2(00) -“retrenchment” means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for 
any reason _ whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action but 
does not include- 


(a) Voluntary retirement of the workman; or 


(b) Retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment 
between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf; or 


(bb) Termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of contract of 
employment between the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract being 
terminated under a stipulation in that behalf contained therein; or 


(c) Termination of the service of a workman on the ground of continued ill-health. 
25-B. Definition of continuous service — For the purpose of —_ this Chapter,- 


(1) a workman shall be said to be in continuous service for a period if he is, for that period, in 
uninterrupted service, including service which may be interrupted on account of sickness or 
authorized leave or an accident or a strike which is not illegal, or a lock-out or a cessation of work 
which is not due to any fault on the part of the workman; 


(2) Where a workman is not in continuous service within the meaning of clause (1) for a period of one 
year or six months, 16 shall be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer- 


(a) for a period one year, if the workman, during a period of twelve calendar months preceding the date 
with reference to which calculation is to be made, has actually worked under the employer for not 
less than — 


(i) one hundred and ninety days in the case of a workman employed below ground in a mine; and 


(ii) two hundred and forty days, in any other case; 


Section 25-F of the Industrial Dispute Act reads as follows:- 


25-F Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen- No workman employed in any industry who 


106 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


has been in continuous service for not less than one year under an _— employer shall be retrenched 
by that employer until- 


(a) The workman has been given one month’s notice in writing indicating the reasons for 
retrenchment and the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of 
such notice, wages for the period of the notice: 


(b) The workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be 
equivalent to fifteen days’ average pay (for Every completed year of continuous service) or any 


part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) Notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government (or such authority as 
may be specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official Gazette.) 


26. In this case it has been held earlier (supra) by this Tribunal that the concerned work-woman Smt. Kalpana 
Pradhan had worked in the Bagadia Branch of UCO Bank, Angul since 26.04.2010 continuously till 19.01.2016 
the date in which she was terminated so she had worked under the management of the Bagadia Branch of UCO 
Bank, Angul for more than 240 days in each and every calendar year. Therefore, the concerned work- woman 
was in continuous service under the management of Bagadia Branch of UCO Bank, Angul as per definition 
mentioned u/s 25-B of I.D. Act. Moreover, there is also evidence that the concerned workman was terminated 
from her service w.e.f. 19.01.2016. Further there is no evidence before the Tribunal that the concerned work- 
woman had been given any notice in writing indicating the reasons for her termination or had been paid 
compensation equivalent to 15 days of average pay as per provision of 25-F of the I.D. Act. 


27. Now, in this case the concerned workman had been engaged on daily wages in the Bagadia Branch of UCO 
Bank for about five years and her service was terminated by the Bagadia Branch of UCO Bank on 19.01.2016 without 
complying the provisions of section 25-F of the I.D. Act. Hence, the action of — the management in terminating the 
services of concerned work-woman w.e.f. 19.01.2016 is not legal and justified. Hence the concerned workman 
is entitled for relief. In view of such the Issue No. I & II are answered in favour of the 27 Party-Work-woman. 


ISSUE NO. 11 


28. After considering all the facts and circumstances it appears that about nine years have elapsed after 
termination of the concerned work-woman in __ the year 2016, so giving relief of reinstatement after long gap would 
not serve any purpose. 


29. In view of such fact the Tribunal comes to the conclusion that it would _ be just, proper and reasonable to 
Award lump-sum monetary compensation to the concerned work-woman in place of her claim of reinstatement 
and other benefits. 


30. Hence, the management of UCO Bank, Bagadia Branch is directed to pay a sum of Rs. 5,00,000 (five 
lakhs) to the concerned workwoman as compensation. The dictates of the award shall be complied with within two 
months from the date of publication of the award failing which the 11 Party-Management shall also be liable to pay 
interest on the amount of | compensation at the rate of 6% per annum. 


Accordingly, this Issue is answered in favour of the 2™ Party-Work- woman. 
31. This is the Award of the Tribunal. The reference is answered accordingly. 


32. Office is directed to send the copy of the Award to the Ministry of Labour for publishing the Award in 
the official gazette.

1. The workman Sh. Ajay Kumar has filed the present claim petition directly under Section 2A of 


the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter called as the Act) claiming his reinstatement with full back 
wages along with consequential benefits. 

2५; It is maintained in the claim petition by the workman that he was appointed as a Rigger under 
respondent 10.1 through respondent no.2 and worked as such w.e.f. 23.10.2015 to 06.09.2017. His services 
were terminated on 07.09.2017 without assigning any reasonable cause. He was drawing Rs.11,500/- per 
month as salary. He has completed more than 240 days in a calendar year from the date of termination. No 
notice was given to him and no inquiry was held by the respondents at the time of his termination. The 
respondents have also appointed juniors to him namely Jai Parkash and Satpal, thus contravened the 
Section 25H of the Act. He represented against his termination, but to no effect. It is prayed that he may be 
reinstated with full back wages and all consequential benefits. 

3. Notice of the claim petition was given to the respondents. 

4. Respondent 10.1 filed reply maintaining therein that the workman was never employed by 
respondent 10.1. Respondent 10.1 being a Public Sector Undertaking employs persons in accordance with 
the recruitment Rules/Regulations/Policies/Instruction of the respondent corporation. The workman never 
applied for any post with respondent no.1 nor he appeared for any written test or interview or trade test for 
recruitment of any post. The workman was never called for any interview, nor he ever underwent any 
medical test. He was never issued any appointment letter or employee number. There is no relationship of 
employer-employee between the management and the workman as the workman was engaged by the 
contractor i.e. respondent no.2. The workman by means of his frivolous and malafide intentions is trying to 
gain a back door entry into a public employment. The management award the contract for work, which is 
non-perennial in nature, non-core, not of sufficient duration, incidental/temporary. After awarding the 
contract, the contractor employs his own workers to carry out the contract and the management has 
absolutely no role in that process. The contract was awarded to the respondent no.2 by executing a formal 


108 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


contract dated 31.07.2015 for 12 months and on expiry of the said contract, the same was duly extended for 
a further period of 12 months on the same terms and conditions and was expired on 31.05.2017. The 
contractor exercises the complete administrative control and supervision over the workers employed by 
him for the performance of his contractual obligation and respondent 10.1 has no role to play in the 
process. The entire service conditions viz. selection, recruitment, appointment, attendance, duty roaster, 
weekly off, shift, leave, wages, ESI, EPF, bonus etc. are managed by the contractor. Hence, question of 
terminating the services of workman or assigning any reasons by respondent no.1 does not arise at all as 
the workman was engaged by respondent no.2. Respondent no.2 had engaged/employed less than 20 
workmen during the entire tenure of the contract, therefore, he was not required to obtain any license for 
engaging/employing workmen for performing the said contract. It is prayed that the claim may be rejected 
with cost. 

5. Respondent 10.2 also filed written statement maintaining therein that it had contract (work 
order) with respondent no.1. As per work order no.24406167, the contract was completed and it had paid 
all the wages to the labour and nothing is pending due of any labour. It is prayed that the case may be 
dismissed. 


Evidence of workman:- 


6 In order to prove case, workman examined himself as WW1 and tendered into evidence his 
affidavit Ex.WW1/A along with documents Ex.WW1/1 (Bank Account Statement), Ex.WW 1/2 (entry cum 
safety pass for contractor’s workers) and Mark A (attendance card). AR for workman closed the evidence 
on behalf of workman on 17.07.2023. 


Evidence of respondent no.1:- 


de Thereafter, respondent 10.1 has examined Sh. P K Sinha, Chief General Manager (Project), 
Indian Oil Corporation Limited Panipat Refinery as MW1, who tendered her affidavit as MWI/A. 
Thereafter, ld. counsel for management closed evidence on 04.04.2025 on behalf of respondent 10.1. He 
relied upon the following documents:-

2: Letter of acceptance 28.03.2015 M-2 
3. Work order 28.03.2015 M-3 
4. Contract agreement 31.07.2015 M-4 
5. Letter of extension of contract 29.04.2016 M-5 
| _ 6. ।[|। Register of wages June 2015 M-6 
7. Register of wages March 2017 M-7 
| 8. Register of wages April 2017 M-8 
8. It is pertinent to mention here that respondent no.2 already ex parte on 04.04.2025. 
9. AR for workman contended that workman worked w.e.f. 23.10.2015 to 06.09.2017 under the 


respondent 10.1 through respondent 10.2 and he was removed from service without assigning any reason 
on 07.09.2017. He was getting salary of Rs.11,500/- per month. The workman has completed more than 
240 days in a calendar year preceding the date of termination and the termination is in violation of Section 
25F of the Act. Further, in place of him, Parkash and Satpal were appointed, which is in violation of 
Section 25H of the Act. 

10. On the other hand, AR for respondent 10.1 contended that workman was never engaged by 
respondent 10.1 and was engaged through contractor i.e. respondent no.2, who was awarded contract by 
respondent 10.1 for its work. Aforesaid contractor is not having license to supply the work force as it was 
engaging less than 20 employees at the time of contract. Thus, no liability of respondent 10.1 is made out 
and therefore, workman is not entitled for any claim from respondent 10.1. Whatever claim made out by 
the workman is against respondent no.2 i.e. contractor, who has already been proceeded ex parte due to 
non-appearance. 

11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 

12. The first contention regarding the claimant is that whether he comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that claimant was appointed as rigger as 
per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the claimant was 
performing his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post 
requiring him to perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme 


Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532, has 
observed as follows:- 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 109 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 
employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment 
are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the 
meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make 
any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on 
contract basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it 
can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for 
doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed 
hours is not a workman.” 
13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make 
any distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is 
nothing in plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular 
basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, 
part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the claimant 
herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 
14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj 
Saluja Vs. Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find 
out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 
1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated 
in the claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of 
wages, salary, letter of appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this 
basic feature for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent no.1 and 
workman totally lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, 
MW1 Sh. PK Sinha in his cross examination has stated that contract for project was given to the 
respondent 10.2 i.e. Ambedkar Construction. The contract was awarded for the period March 2015 to 
March 2017. Payment to the employees of the contractor was paid by the contractor. EPF and ESI were 
paid by the contractor and not by the respondent no.1. Supervision and control of workers remained with 
the contractor. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 
16. It is also added here that respondent no.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.M1 to Ex.M8. 
Ex.M4 is the contract agreement and Ex.MS5 is the extension of contract and Ex.M6 to Ex.M8 are the 
register of wages. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was paid salary by the 
contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist any 
relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists 
relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 
17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 
was supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, he would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 
“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. 
Rajappa 1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in 
Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is 
industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between 
employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or 
distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an 
“Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent no.1 at 
the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which 
involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 

19. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F of 
the Act. To prove this, he come to the witness box and stated that he has worked with Ambedkar 


110 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Construction since September 2015 to September 2017. Thus, there was non-compliance of Section 25F of 
the Act and for that respondent no.2 is liable. However, it is added here that currently contractor is not 
working with the respondent no.2. Thus only remedy left with the Tribunal is to grant compensation to the 
workman. 

20. In view of above discussion, keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and 
salary given to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of 
the Act, this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that workman is entitled for compensation of Rs.50,000/- 
and respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.50,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from 
the date of award till the date of making payment.

1. The workman Sh. Umesh Kumar has filed the present claim petition directly under Section 2A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter called as the Act) claiming his reinstatement with full 
back wages along with consequential benefits. 

2. It is maintained in the claim petition by the workman that he was appointed as a Rigger under 
respondent 10.1 through respondent 10.2 and worked as such w.e.f. 23.10.2015 to 06.09.2017. His services 
were terminated on 07.09.2017 without assigning any reasonable cause. He was drawing Rs.11,500/- per 
month as salary. He has completed more than 240 days in a calendar year from the date of termination. No 
notice was given to him and no inquiry was held by the respondents at the time of his termination. The 
respondents have also appointed juniors to him namely Jai Parkash and Satpal, thus contravened the 
Section 25H of the Act. He represented against his termination, but to no effect. It is prayed that he may be 
reinstated with full back wages and all consequential benefits. 

3. Notice of the claim petition was given to the respondents. 

4. Respondent 10.1 filed reply maintaining therein that the workman was never employed by 
respondent 10.1. Respondent 10.1 being a Public Sector Undertaking employs persons in accordance with 
the recruitment Rules/Regulations/Policies/Instruction of the respondent corporation. The workman never 
applied for any post with respondent 10.1 nor he appeared for any written test or interview or trade test for 
recruitment of any post. The workman was never called for any interview, nor he ever underwent any 
medical test. He was never issued any appointment letter or employee number. There is no relationship of 
employer-employee between the management and the workman as the workman was engaged by the 
contractor i.e. respondent no.2. The workman by means of his frivolous and malafide intentions is trying to 
gain a back door entry into a public employment. The management award the contract for work, which is 
non-perennial in nature, non-core, not of sufficient duration, incidental/temporary. After awarding the 
contract, the contractor employs his own workers to carry out the contract and the management has 
absolutely no role in that process. The contract was awarded to the respondent no.2 by executing a formal 
contract dated 31.07.2015 for 12 months and on expiry of the said contract, the same was duly extended for 
a further period of 12 months on the same terms and conditions and was expired on 31.05.2017. The 
contractor exercises the complete administrative control and supervision over the workers employed by 
him for the performance of his contractual obligation and respondent 10.1 has no role to play in the 
process. The entire service conditions viz. selection, recruitment, appointment, attendance, duty roaster, 
weekly off, shift, leave, wages, ESI, EPF, bonus etc. are managed by the contractor. Hence, question of 
terminating the services of workman or assigning any reasons by respondent no.1 does not arise at all as 
the workman was engaged by respondent no.2. Respondent no.2 had engaged/employed less than 20 
workmen during the entire tenure of the contract, therefore, he was not required to obtain any license for 
engaging/employing workmen for performing the said contract. It is prayed that the claim may be rejected 
with cost. 

5. Respondent 10.2 also filed written statement maintaining therein that it had contract (work 
order) with respondent no.1. As per work order no.24406167, the contract was completed and it had paid 
all the wages to the labour and nothing is pending due of any labour. It is prayed that the case may be 
dismissed. 


Evidence of workman:- 


6 In order to prove case, workman examined himself as WW1 and tendered into evidence his 
affidavit Ex.WW1/A along with documents Ex.WW1/1 (Bank Account Statement), Ex.WW1/2 (entry cum 
safety pass for contractor’s workers) and Mark A (attendance card). AR for workman closed the evidence 
on behalf of workman on 17.07.2023. 


Evidence of respondent no.1:- 


hs Thereafter, respondent 10.1 has examined Sh. P K Sinha, Chief General Manager (Project), 

Indian Oil Corporation Limited Panipat Refinery as MW1, who tendered her affidavit as MWI/A. 

Thereafter, ld. counsel for management closed evidence on 04.04.2025 on behalf of respondent 10.1. He 

relied upon the following documents:-

9. AR for workman contended that workman worked w.e.f. 23.10.2015 to 06.09.2017 under the 


respondent 10.1 through respondent no.2 and he was removed from service without assigning any reason 
on 07.09.2017. He was getting salary of Rs.11,500/- per month. The workman has completed more than 
240 days in a calendar year preceding the date of termination and the termination is in violation of Section 
25F of the Act. Further, in place of him, Jai Parkash and Satpal were appointed, which is in violation of 
Section 25H of the Act. 

10. On the other hand, AR for respondent 10.1 contended that workman was never engaged by 
respondent 10.1 and was engaged through contractor i.e. respondent no.2, who was awarded contract by 
respondent 10.1 for its work. Aforesaid contractor is not having license to supply the work force as it was 
engaging less than 20 employees at the time of contract. Thus, no liability of respondent no.1 is made out 
and therefore, workman is not entitled for any claim from respondent 10.1. Whatever claim made out by

non-appearance. 

11. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by AR for both the parties. 

12. The first contention regarding the claimant is that whether he comes within the definition of 
workman as is defined in Section 2(s) of the Act. I may mention that claimant was appointed as rigger as 
per his claim petition and affidavit submitted before the Tribunal. In plain words the claimant was 
performing his duties as labourer/unskilled worker. He was not in supervisory or administrative post 
requiring him to perform only administrative duties. While interpreting Section 2(s) Hon’ble Supreme 


Court in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2011 Supreme Court 2532, has 
observed as follows:- 


“The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 
employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment 
are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the 
meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make 
any distinction between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on 
contract basis. There is nothing in the plain language of Section 2(s) from which it 
can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person employed for 
doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or 
contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed 
hours is not a workman.” 
13. Thus Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that the definition of workman also does not make 
any distinction between full time or part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is 
nothing in plain language of Section 2(s) from which it can be infer that only person employed on regular 
basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, 
part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a 
workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the claimant 
herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 
14. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj 
Saluja Vs. Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find 
out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 
1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


15. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated 
in the claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of 
wages, salary, letter of appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this 
basic feature for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and 
workman totally lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, 
MW1 Sh. PK Sinha in his cross examination has stated that contract for project was given to the 
respondent no.2 i.e. Ambedkar Construction. The contract was awarded for the period March 2015 to 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 113 


March 2017. Payment to the employees of the contractor was paid by the contractor. EPF and ESI were 
paid by the contractor and not by the respondent 10.1. Supervision and control of workers remained with 
the contractor. Thus, it was the respondent no.2 who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the 
workers engaged by him from time to time. 
16. It is also added here that respondent no.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.M1 to Ex.M8. 
Ex.M4 is the contract agreement and Ex.MS5 is the extension of contract and Ex.M6 to Ex.M8 are the 
register of wages. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was paid salary by the 
contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not exist any 
relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.1. However, there exists 
relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 
17. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 
was supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, he would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 
“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


18. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. 
Rajappa 1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in 
Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is 
industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between 
employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or 
distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an 
“Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent 10.1 at 
the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which 
involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 

19. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F of 
the Act. To prove this, he come to the witness box and stated that he has worked with Ambedkar 
Construction since 23.10.2015 to September 2017. Thus, there was non-compliance of Section 25F of the 
Act and for that respondent 10.2 is liable. However, it is added here that currently contractor is not working 
with the respondent no.2. Thus only remedy left with the Tribunal is to grant compensation to the 
workman. 

20. In view of above discussion, keeping in view the tenure of service rendered by the workman and 
salary given to him during the period of his stay with the contractor and non-compliance of Section 25F of

and respondent no.2 is directed to pay the workman Rs.50,000/- within one month from the date of the 
notification of the award failing which the respondent no.2 shall further pay interest @6% per annum from 
the date of award till the date of making payment.

workman. In view of the ratio of law enunciated in the above ruling, in my considered opinion the claimant 
herein admittedly falls within the definition of ‘workman’ under Section 2(s) of the Act. 
13. The Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj 
Saluja Vs. Air India Limited in Civil Appeal No.10266 dated 25.08.2014, two well recognized tests to find 
out whether the labours are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 

1) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 

2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


14. The facts regarding the payment of salary by the management or contractor has not been stated 
in the claim petition of the workman. In fact, claim petition is totally silent regarding the payment of 
wages, salary, letter of appointment by respondent 10.1 or by contractor or anything likewise. Thus, this 
basic feature for holding the relationship of employer and employee i.e. between respondent 10.1 and 
workman totally lacking not in the pleading but also in the evidence submitted by the workman. However, 
७४] Sh. Ujjwal Mishra in his cross examination has stated that contract for project was given to the 
respondent no.2 i.e. M/s Indus Project Ltd. The contract was awarded for the period from April 2015 for 18 
months which was extended from time to time and is still continuing. Payment to the employees of the 
contractor was paid by the contractor. EPF and ESI were paid by the contractor and not by the respondent 
10.1. Supervision and control of workers remained with the contractor. Thus, it was the respondent 10.2, 
who was required to ensure the payment of wages to the workers engaged by him from time to time. 
15. It is also added here that respondent 10.1 has also placed on record documents Ex.M1 to Ex.M8. 
Ex.MS is the contract agreement. Thus, from the adduced evidence, it emerges that workman was paid 
salary by the contractor and he was being controlled and supervised by the contractor. Thus, there does not 
exist any relationship of employee and employer between the workman and respondent no.1. However, 
there exists relation of employee and employer between the workman and respondent 10.2. 
16. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the 
Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 
was supplying contract labour to the respondent 10.1. Thus, he would fall under the definition of 
contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract Act is reproduced as under: 
“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to 
produce a given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or 
articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies 
contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


17. The Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. 
Rajappa 1978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in 
Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is 
industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between 
employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or 
distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an 
“Industry” in that enterprise. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent no.1 at 
the asking of respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which 
involve substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, respondent 
no.2 would be termed as industry. 

18. Workman in his deposition has clearly stated that there was non-compliance of Section 25F of 
the Act. To prove this, he has stated in his affidavit that he has worked with respondent no.2 from 
09.04.2016 to 31.08.2019. Thus, there was non-compliance of Section 25F of the Act and for that 
respondent no.2 is liable. Since, respondent no.2 is still working with the respondent no.1, so due to non- 
compliance of Section 25F of the Act, workman is entitled for reinstatement. 


19. Hon'ble Apex Court in the case General Manager, Haryana Roadways Vs. Rudan Singh, 
reported as 2005 SCC (L&S)_716 observed as under :- 


"8. There is no rule of thumb that in every case where the Industrial Tribunal gives a 
finding that the termination of service was in violation of Section 25-F of the Act, entire 
back wages should be awarded. A host of factors like the manner and method of selection 
appointment i.e. whether after proper and advertisement of the vacancy or inviting 
applications from the employment exchange, nature of appointment namely, whether ad 
hoc, short term, daily wage, temporary or permanent in character, any special 
qualification required for the job and the like should be weighed and balanced in taking 
a decision regarding award of back wages. One of the important factors which has to be 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 117 


taken into consideration is the length of service, which the workman had rendered with 
the employer. If the workman has rendered a considerable period of service and his 
services are wrongfully terminated, he may be awarded full or partial back wages 
keeping in view the fact that at this age and the qualification possessed by him he may 
not be in a position to get another employment. However, where the total length of 
service rendered by a workman is very small, the award of back wages for the complete 
period i.e. from the date of termination till the date of the award, which our experience 
shows is often quite large, would be wholly inappropriate. A regular service of 
permanent character cannot be compared to short or intermittent daily wage employment 
though it may be for 240 days in a calendar year.”’ 


20. Having regard to the legal position as discussed above and the facts, this Tribunal is of the firm 
view that the workman has been terminated without following the procedure laid down under Section 25F 
of the Act. It is pertinent to mention that he has specifically not pleaded that he is not working anywhere. 
Moreover, nothing has been asked from this witness regarding his employment/termination as such, it 
cannot be decided conclusively with respect to his future employment after the alleged termination. Hence, 
the workman is entitled for reinstatement into service on the same post from the date of his termination 
with 50% back wages in as much as termination of workman is per-se illegal. Respondent 10.2 is directed 
to pay 50% back wages and reinstate the workman forthwith. 


21. Let copy of this award be sent to Central Government for publication as required under Section 
17 of the Act. 


KAMAL KANT, Presiding Officer

The Central Government, Ministry of Labour& Employment vide its Order

adjudication. 

The schedule mentioned in that order is: 
“Whether the demand raised by the petitioner union (Tamilnadu General Workers Union, Chennai Airport Contract 


Workers Unit, Chennai) against the respondent management (M/s Airports Authority of India, Chennai and their 
Contractors M/s BVG India Limited, M/s QPMS, M/s Aroon Aviation Services P Ltd) to provide 12 days casual leave 


[भाग 1---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 119 


per year, earned leave and medical leave is legal and justified? If not, to what relief the petitioner union is entitled 
to?” 

2. Onreceipt of the above reference dated 03.12.2024 from the appropriate Government, the dispute was 
registered as ID No. 110/2024 and due notices were issued to both the parties for their appearance fixing the case to 
19.02.2025. Neither the Petitioner nor any Counsel / Authorized Representative turned up resulting further 
adjournments to 14.05.2025, 14.07.2025, 01.09.2025 and 27.10.2025. The Petitioner did not turn up whereas the 
Respondent No.1 and 2 filed Vakalat Namas. It reveals from the body of reference that while the appropriate Govt. 
sent the reference dated 03.12.2024 to this Tribunal for adjudication, copies of the reference were sent to the 
Petitioner and all the opposite parties. It is therefore well presumed that both parties must have received the 
reference. Even then, in the interest of justice, the Petitioner was once again directed to appear and to file claim 
statement fixing the case to 22.12.2025. The Petitioner did not turn up nor was any authorized representative of the 
counsel on his behalf present. The claim statement was not furnished in any manner by the Petitioner. The 
Respondents (1२1 and R2) were present. It reveals the Petitioner, despite of sufficient opportunity choose not to appear 
or to file claim statement and documents. 


3. In the circumstance it deems proper not to re-list the case for the same purpose to any other date which 
would be wastage of the valuable time of this Tribunal. The case was reserved for Final Order.

the case. Thus, the Tribunal is not in a position to adjudicate the dispute as referred by the Appropriate Government,

ORDER 


This petition has been filed by the Petitioner against the Respondent Management under section 33-C (2) of 
the Industrial Dispute Act 1947 which is corresponding section 59 (2) under the Industrial Relation Code 2020 for the 
recovery of the amount of Rs.83,630.77/- with regard to legitimate dues of full and final payments including 
retrenchment allowances as per contract. 


2, Petitioner in his petition has averred that the 17 Respondent Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, got registered itself 
as Principal Employer under Central Legislative Enactment, "Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970." 
(Annexure 13) dated 14" August 2009, and (Annexure 14) dated 29" July 2011. The ps Respondent "Midfield 
Industries Limited," is licensed contractor under the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, and copy 
of the license is Annexure 17, dated 197 August 2009, confirming that the 27 Respondent is licensed to work as a 
contractor in the 1“ Respondent industry establishment at Visakhapatnam. The 3™ Respondent "M/s Rishita 
Associates," is also licensed contractor by Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970, and the license 
issued to the 37 Respondent is (Annexure 15) dated 67 November 2000. Further, Petitioner has averred that 1“ 
Respondent acknowledged and accepted the 37 Respondent, Rishita Associates, as sub-contractor for the 20 
Respondent, Midfield Industries Limited, vide annexure 12, dated 157 September 2009. The 2" Respondent and 3" 
Respondent are licensed to work for the first Respondent, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, at Visakhapatnam. Further, it is 
averred that the 11 Respondent issued the work order to the 27 Respondent vide work contract, dated 127 September 
2009, under later of acceptance by the 271 Respondent, vide (Annexure 7) and the 2" Respondent accepted the work 
contract initially for a period of 24 months from 16" August 2009, and later it was extended for another 12 months, 
vide letter dated 177 October 2012, confirming the work contract extension up to 15"" August 2012, by (Annexure 
8). Further, Petitioner averred that the 27 Respondent who engaged the Petitioner workmen as contact labour upon 
receiving the work contract (Annexure 7), later shifted all contact labour to the 31 Respondent vide agreement 
between the 2" and 37 Respondents meant to execute work order of the 1“ Respondent dated 120 September 2009. 
According to (Annexure 11) which is the agreement between the 21 Respondent, "Midfield Industries Limited," and 
371 Respondent, "Rishita Associates," dated 12.9.2009 for the work order dated 167 August 2009, and same _ is 
binding agreement/settlement between the 276 and 3 Respondents and is the foundation for the claim application 
for the recovery of the arrears as settled under (Annexure 11) settlement. Further, Petitioner has contended that 
Annexure-20 confirms that the 37 Respondent Rishita Associates, received photo gate pass under (Annexure 11) in 


[भाग Ive 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जनवरी 24, 2026/माघ 4, 1947 121 


favour of the 86-contract labour including the Petitioner engaged by the 317 Respondent between the period of 
contract, i.e., 16” August 2009, to 157 August 2012, for 36 months on behalf of the 978 Respondent and (Annexure 
20) is the photo identity gate pass cancellation order issued by 1“ Respondent for 86 contract labour upon completion 
of the work contract. Further, it is averred that the Petitioner workmen are entitled to receive wages and terminal 
benefits upon the completion of the work contract, as contracted and settled under (annexure 11) between the second 
and 3rd Respondents for executing the work contract of the first Respondent and Petitioner is entitled to receive 
retrenchment allowances for contract labour at the rate of "actual working days/26 x month" 8 days. The Petitioner 
is unskilled and is entitled for the arrear of the amount due to words notice pay, service pay, and leave pay for 900 
working days, amounting to Rs.83,633.77/-. Since both third Respondent as well as the 27 Respondent failed to pay 
the terminal benefits upon the completion of the work contract on 15" August 2012, Petitioner workman demanded 
the legal dues with interest from all Respondent collectively but they did not pay. Further, it is submitted that after a 
lapse of nearly 15 months, 2" Respondent addressed a letter to the 1 Respondent (annexure 19) to make all the 
labour benefits payments directly to the workman such of that amount to be cleared against the work contract dated 
12" September 2009, from pending amount due to the 2" Respondent's account with the 1“ Respondent. 1“ 
Respondent acknowledged the letter, but no payment was made. Moreover, Petitioner union also addressed a letter 
(annexure 6) dated 247 March 2014, directly to 1st Respondent to release all the contract labour legal dues, and 1“ 
Respondent acknowledged the same but it was in vain. Further, it is averred that the 27 Respondent, vide (annexure 
5) dated 127 January 2015, addressed letter to the 1‘ Respondent requesting to settle all legal dues to the Petitioner 
contract labour and 1* Respondent acknowledged the receipt of this letter but did not pay dues. Further, all the 
contract labour including Petitioner made representation through their union before the Regional Labour 
Commissioner Central Vishakhapatnam, vide (annexure 3) dated 19" August 2015, and (annexure 4) dated 207 July 
2015. The concerned authority issued notices to all Respondents, but no relief was granted to the workman. 
Therefore, Petitioner has moved this petition under section 33C (2) of the ID Act for recovery of his legitimate dues 
from Respondent. Petitioner submitted that the 17 Respondent is legally bound to pay all the legal dues to the contract 
labour vide (Annexure 13) the undertaking given by the 17 Respondent, and under section 21(4) of the Contract 
Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970 and Petitioner is also entitled to receive all the legitimate dues with 
interest at the rate of 18% per annum. 


3. Notice were issued to all Respondent. Respondent No.1 and Respondent No. 3 has filed their counter, but 
Respondent No. 2 did not file any counter despite service of notice. Therefore, case is proceeding ex-parte against 27 
Respondent. 


4. In response to notice Respondent No. 1 has filed counter and therein, he has contended that the petition filed 
by the Petitioner is not maintainable and is liable to be dismissed in limine. Further, it is contended that this 
Respondent awarded a contract to the 2" Respondent, Midfield Industry Limited, Hyderabad, a licensed contractor 
for the work of "strapping of mill products” vide work order No. VSP/WC/WRM/58485-0/OT/2009- 10/8090000359 
dated 12" August 2009, for the period of 24 month, commencing from 167 August 2009 to 15" August 2011. This 
contract was further extended for another period of 12 months with effect from 16" August 2011 to 15" August 2012. 
The 2™ Respondent contractor vide letter dated 12" August 2009, requested Respondent No. 1 to permit it to engage 
M/s Rishita Associates, Vishakhapatnam, sub/contractor, for supply of the labour for the subject contract work. 1“ 
Respondent considered request made by the 2" Respondent-contractor and, vide its letter dated 157 September 2009,

15"" September 2009, 11 Respondent clearly mentioned that clearance approved by it for engaging sub-contractor

Vishakhapatnam Steel Plant. It was clarified further that 2"' Respondent contractor is not relieved from the 
Contractual obligations, responsibilities, and liabilities, etc. Further, Respondent contended that 86 contract labour 
are the contract labour of M/s Midfield Industries. The 2" Respondent and as per the approval given by this

Employer/RINI, claiming reimbursement of the same. Respondent contended that third Respondent/sub- 
contractor/Rishita Associates had paid the wages to the contract labour for the total contract period after expiry of the 
contract period with the second Respondent, and entire contract labour including the Petitioner herein continued to 
work under a new contractor for the same work as the work of Strapping of Mill Products in WRM" is a continuous 
process. Further, it is submitted that second Respondent/contractor/Mid Field Industries submitted a request to RINL 
stating that it is entangled in income tax problems and requested to make payment in full and final due to its 
contractor labour, from out of the amounts due to it and pending with RINL. Accordingly, after obtaining due 
approvals and based on the amount due it was released by 1“ Respondent/RINL to 275 Respondent/contractor paid an 
amount of Rs.28.58.522/- to the contract labour towards partial disbursement of terminal benefits. A copy of the 
payment particulars to contract labour in enclosed herewith and Petitioner has been paid Rs. 33,272/- out of the 


122 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JANUARY 24, 2026/MAGHA 4, 1947 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


amount of Rs. 46,836/-. The 2™ Respondent/contractor addressed a Letter di 19.02.2014 requesting the Principal 
Employer/RINL to release the amount equivalent to full and final amount as a special case by making partial 
modifications to the agreement entered between it and 17 Respondent/RINL. Respondent made several reminders to

Respondent/RINL processed the bill exparte. Respondent contended that as directions issued by the Income Tax

dues to be paid to the Income Tax Department from the pending bills of the second Respondent/contractor M/s

Department. Further, Respondent contended that the terminal benefit claimed by the Petitioner does not form part of 
wages and, as such the contractor as a direct employer is legally responsible to make all other payments if any to the 
Petitioner. Therefore, the petition is devoid of any merit and not legally maintainable, and it is liable to be dismissed. 


3: Respondent No. 2 did not turn up despite service of notice and nor filed any counter. Therefore, case is 
proceeding ex-parte against Respondent No. 2 vide order dated 20" September 2017 and being heard and decided 
exparte. 


6. Respondent No. 3 has filed his counter and therein it is contended that the averments made by the Petitioner 
in the petition are not true, valid, tenable, and petition filed by the Petitioner under section 33C(2) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act is not maintainable under law, as no amount is due and payable by this Respondent to the Petitioner. 
Further, Respondent No.3 contended that the first Respondent Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited/Visakhapatnam Steel 
Plant vide its Work Order dated 12th September 2009 awarded a contract for the work of "Scrapping of Mill Products 
in Wire Rod MHL to the second Respondent/Midfield Industries Limited, Hyderabad. Initially, contract period to 
work was for 24 months from 16.08.2009 to 15.08 2011 and later on it was extended for further period of 12 months 
commencing from 16.08.2011 to 15.08.2012. Further, it is contended that after obtaining approval from the first 
Respondent/ RINL, 2" Respondent/Midfield Industries Limited of labour to carry out the contract work entrusted the 
work to Respondent No.3 on sub-contract basis i.e. for supply of contract labour between the first Respondent/RINL 
and second Respondent, work on commission basis and this Respondent has no other role in respect of Midfield 
Industries Ltd. While approving/permitting the second Respondent for giving the work to this Respondent on sub- 
contract basis, the first Respondent has clearly stated in their Letter dt. 15.09.2009 that the permission for engaging 
the sub-contractor does not establish or create between their Respondent and 21 Respondent/Midfield Industries 
Limited any contractual relationship or obligation between RINL and Respondent No. 2 is not relieved from the 
contractual obligations, liabilities and other responsibilities and he is alone responsible for any claim. This clearly 
establish that any dispute or claim by any third party, the first Respondent a Principal Employer and the Second 
Respondent as main Contractor are liable/responsible, and this Respondent is not liable for any claim made by the

11. Perused the record. At the outset, Respondent counsel urged that present petition filed by the Petitioner for 
the recovery of full and final payment amounting to Rs.83,630.77 ps. along with the interest for the work under 
contract is not maintainable under section 33-C(2) of ID Act 1947 as there is no amount due to the Petitioner from 
Respondent. 


Firstly, we have to examine provision contained under section 33 C (2) of the ID Act. Section 33 C (2) of ID Act 
provides :- 


"Where any workman is entitled to receive from the employer any money or any benefit which is capable of being 
computed in terms of money, and if any question arises as to the amount of money due or as to the amount at 
which such benefit should be computed, then the question may, subject to any rules that may be wait under this 
act, be decided by such labour court as may be specified in this behalf by the appropriate government within a 
period of not exceeding three month." 


12. Thus, in view of provision contained u/s 33-C (2) we proceed to examine the question whether the Petitioner 
is entitle to receive from employer any money or benefit which is capable of being computed in terms of money. In 
this context Petitioner has filed documents in evidence which has been exhibited by witness WW1. The perusal of 
these document reveals that the document Ex.W1 is the form of certificate issued by principal employer i.e., Deputy 
General Manager, Visakhapatnam Steel Plant, Visakhapatnam to the effect that it has engaged M/s. Midfield 
industries Ltd Respondent No.2 for the work of strapping of mill product in WRM as contractor at Steel Plant, 
Visakhapatnam vide certificate dated 14" August, 2009. Further, Document Ex.W8 is the letter dated 157 
September, 2009, issued by AGM works contract of Respondent No.1 addressed to M/s. Midfield Industries Limited.
